question: How did the banks do in the stress test?
answer:
In the 2026 Federal Reserve Stress Test (results released June 24, 2026), the 32 large banks subject to the test performed well: they have sufficient capital to absorb nearly $708 billion in losses and continue lending under the severely adverse scenario, with all aggregate and individual post-stress capital ratios staying above required regulatory minimums throughout the projection horizon [D1][D8].

**Overall (aggregate) results**
- The aggregate common equity tier 1 (CET1) ratio of the 32 banks fell from an actual 12.8% in 2025:Q4 to a projected minimum of 11.2%, before recovering to 12.7% by 2028:Q1 [D1][D8][D15].
- The 1.6 percentage point aggregate CET1 decline was smaller than in recent years [D9].
- Other aggregate stressed minimums: Tier 1 capital 12.6%, total capital 14.8%, Tier 1 leverage 6.7%, and supplementary leverage 5.5% (versus actual 2025:Q4 levels of 14.2%, 16.2%, 7.6%, and 6.3%, respectively) [D15].
- Projected aggregate loan losses were $625 billion (a 6.9% loan loss rate), with provisions for loan and lease losses of $635 billion; commercial loans were 48% of total losses, consumer loans 41%, and credit cards the largest single portfolio at 29% [D19].
- Drivers of this year's results: greater loan losses (2025 loan balances grew ~10%, concentrated in credit cards and wholesale loans, plus more severe corporate bond spread and commercial real estate price paths), smaller unrealized gains on available-for-sale securities (smaller projected interest rate declines), and higher net interest income [D9].

**Bank-by-bank projected minimum CET1 ratios (severely adverse, 2026:Q1–2028:Q1)**
Individual banks ranged from a low of 6.7% (First Citizens) to a high of 32.2% (Charles Schwab Corp) [D4][D16].

| Highest buffers | Min CET1 | | Lowest buffers | Min CET1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Charles Schwab Corp | 32.2% | | First Citizens | 6.7% |
| UBS Americas | 15.3% | | Ally | 7.8% |
| DB USA | 14.4% | | HSBC North America | 8.1% |
| TD Group US | 14.0% | | Citizens Financial Group | 8.6% |
| RBC US Group | 13.7% | | Wells Fargo | 9.2% |

Among the largest U.S. domestic banks, JPMorgan Chase (12.6%) and Morgan Stanley (12.5%) had the highest buffers, while Ally (7.8%) and HSBC (8.1%) had the lowest [D4][D16]. The full set of 32 bank-level ratios is available in the results table [D4][D16].

**Year-over-year comparison**
- The official (risk-weighted) aggregate minimum CET1 was 11.2% for the 32 banks in 2026, versus 11.6% for the 22 banks in 2025 — a 0.4 percentage point decline [D6].
- The simple (unweighted) average of bank-level minimum CET1 ratios was 11.47% in 2026 (32 banks) versus 12.21% in 2025 (22 banks) [D5]. Note the participant count rose from 22 to 32, so the two years are not directly comparable on a like-for-like basis.

**Resulting capital requirements**
The Board voted in February 2026 to maintain current stress capital buffer (SCB) requirements until 2027, so the June 2026 capital requirements document shows no changes from 2025; new entrants receive a 2.5% SCB [D8][D10]. Total CET1 requirements equal the 4.5% minimum plus the SCB plus any GSIB surcharge. Examples: JPMorgan Chase 11.5% (4.5 + 2.5 + 4.5), Citigroup 11.6% (4.5 + 3.6 + 3.5), Morgan Stanley 11.8% (4.5 + 4.3 + 3.0), Goldman Sachs 11.4% (4.5 + 3.4 + 3.5), Bank of America 10.0% (4.5 + 2.5 + 3.0), DB USA 16.0% (4.5 + 11.5), and Wells Fargo 8.5% (4.5 + 2.5 + 1.5) [D12][D14].

One caveat: because the Board held SCB requirements flat, the 2026 stress test results did not inform the current SCB requirements; for banks that did not participate in the 2025 test, the SCB is based on 2024 results [D12].

args.sql:
SELECT disclosure_legal_name, common_equity_tier1_min_rat
FROM dfast_results_2013_2026
WHERE exercise_name = '2026 Stress Test'
  AND scenario_name = 'Supervisory Severely Adverse'
ORDER BY common_equity_tier1_min_rat DESC

SELECT exercise_name,
       COUNT(*) AS n_banks,
       AVG(common_equity_tier1_min_rat) AS avg_min_cet1
FROM dfast_results_2013_2026
WHERE exercise_name IN ('2025 Stress Test','2026 Stress Test')
  AND scenario_name = 'Supervisory Severely Adverse'
  AND disclosure_legal_name NOT ILIKE '%participating%'
  AND disclosure_legal_name NOT ILIKE '%bank holding companies%'
  AND disclosure_legal_name NOT ILIKE '%firms%'
GROUP BY exercise_name
ORDER BY exercise_name

- The aggregate common equity tier 1 (CET1) ratio of the 32 banks fell from an actual 12.8% in 2025:Q4 to a projected minimum of 11.2%, before recovering to 12.7% by 2028:Q1 [D1][D8][D15].
- The 1.6 percentage point aggregate CET1 decline was smaller than in recent years [D9].
- Other aggregate stressed minimums: Tier 1 capital 12.6%, total capital 14.8%, Tier 1 leverage 6.7%, and supplementary leverage 5.5% (versus actual 2025:Q4 levels of 14.2%, 16.2%, 7.6%, and 6.3%, respectively) [D15].
- Projected aggregate loan losses were $625 billion (a 6.9% loan loss rate), with provisions for loan and lease losses of $635 billion; commercial loans were 48% of total losses, consumer loans 41%, and credit cards the largest single portfolio at 29% [D19].
- Drivers of this year's results: greater loan losses (2025 loan balances grew ~10%, concentrated in credit cards and wholesale loans, plus more severe corporate bond spread and commercial real estate price paths), smaller unrealized gains on available-for-sale securities (smaller projected interest rate declines), and higher net interest income [D9].

**Bank-by-bank projected minimum CET1 ratios (severely adverse, 2026:Q1–2028:Q1)**
Individual banks ranged from a low of 6.7% (First Citizens) to a high of 32.2% (Charles Schwab Corp) [D4][D16].

| Highest buffers | Min CET1 | | Lowest buffers | Min CET1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Charles Schwab Corp | 32.2% | | First Citizens | 6.7% |
| UBS Americas | 15.3% | | Ally | 7.8% |
| DB USA | 14.4% | | HSBC North America | 8.1% |
| TD Group US | 14.0% | | Citizens Financial Group | 8.6% |
| RBC US Group | 13.7% | | Wells Fargo | 9.2% |

Among the largest U.S. domestic banks, JPMorgan Chase (12.6%) and Morgan Stanley (12.5%) had the highest buffers, while Ally (7.8%) and HSBC (8.1%) had the lowest [D4][D16]. The full set of 32 bank-level ratios is available in the results table [D4][D16].

**Year-over-year comparison**
- The official (risk-weighted) aggregate minimum CET1 was 11.2% for the 32 banks in 2026, versus 11.6% for the 22 banks in 2025 — a 0.4 percentage point decline [D6].
- The simple (unweighted) average of bank-level minimum CET1 ratios was 11.47% in 2026 (32 banks) versus 12.21% in 2025 (22 banks) [D5]. Note the participant count rose from 22 to 32, so the two years are not directly comparable on a like-for-like basis.

**Resulting capital requirements**
The Board voted in February 2026 to maintain current stress capital buffer (SCB) requirements until 2027, so the June 2026 capital requirements document shows no changes from 2025; new entrants receive a 2.5% SCB [D8][D10]. Total CET1 requirements equal the 4.5% minimum plus the SCB plus any GSIB surcharge. Examples: JPMorgan Chase 11.5% (4.5 + 2.5 + 4.5), Citigroup 11.6% (4.5 + 3.6 + 3.5), Morgan Stanley 11.8% (4.5 + 4.3 + 3.0), Goldman Sachs 11.4% (4.5 + 3.4 + 3.5), Bank of America 10.0% (4.5 + 2.5 + 3.0), DB USA 16.0% (4.5 + 11.5), and Wells Fargo 8.5% (4.5 + 2.5 + 1.5) [D12][D14].

One caveat: because the Board held SCB requirements flat, the 2026 stress test results did not inform the current SCB requirements; for banks that did not participate in the 2025 test, the SCB is based on 2024 results [D12].

question: Is inflation coming down?
answer:
Taking "is inflation coming down?" to mean the current trend in U.S. headline and core CPI/PCE over the last several months, and the "latest Fed view" to mean the September 15–16, 2026 FOMC meeting and the July 2026 Monetary Policy Report: **No — by the Fed's preferred measures, inflation is not coming down; it re-accelerated sharply in spring 2026 and remains well above the 2% goal, which is why the Committee hiked rates on September 16, 2026.** The one bright spot is core CPI, which has been falling steadily.

## What the data show (latest readings: August 2026)

Headline and core PCE — the measures the Fed emphasizes — are still elevated and only modestly off their spring peaks:

| Measure (YoY) | Jun 2025 | Peak (May 2026) | Latest (Aug 2026) | Trend |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Headline CPI | 2.68% | 4.17% | 3.35% | Up, then partial pullback [M4] |
| Headline PCE | 2.61% | 3.82% | 3.42% | Up, then partial pullback [M3] |
| Core PCE (Fed's preferred) | 2.83% | 3.16% | 3.01% | Up, then partial pullback [M5] |
| Core CPI | 2.91% | 3.11% (Aug 2025) | 2.45% | Steadily down, 14-month low [M6] |

So the picture is mixed: headline and core PCE spiked from mid-2025 to a May 2026 high and have eased somewhat over the last three months, but they remain far above 2%. Core CPI is the exception, declining from 3.11% (Aug 2025) to 2.45% (Aug 2026), its lowest level in the 14-month period for which data is available [M6]. Month-over-month, headline measures jumped in Feb–Mar 2026 (CPI +0.87%/+0.64%; PCE +0.63%/+0.44%), turned negative in June (CPI −0.42%; PCE −0.10%), and ticked back up in July–August [M7][M8]. Note the latest available data is for August 2026; September 2026 readings are not yet out (expected mid-October 2026).

## What the latest Fed documents say

**September 16, 2026 FOMC statement** (12–0 vote, a 25 bp hike to 3¾–4%): "Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability." [D3] Notably, the statement does *not* use the softer "moving toward 2 percent" or "disinflationary progress" language — the framing is "elevated" plus a commitment to a "timelier return."

**Chair Warsh's press conference (Sept 16, 2026)** was more emphatic: "inflation is too high and has been for too long," and "This summer's inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved." He cited total PCE around 3.6% in August, core PCE about 3.2%, and CPI about 2.4%, with "too many categories" still rising above 3% on 6- and 12-month bases [D5]. He said the standard for easing — being "confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed" — "has not been satisfied" [D6]. On the Summary of Economic Projections, he noted median total PCE inflation of 3.7% this year falling to 2.3% next year, with "inflation risks to the upside" [D6]. When asked how a "timelier return" squares with the median pushing 2% out to 2029, Warsh stressed those were his colleagues' forecasts, not his own, and reaffirmed the commitment to deliver price stability [D10].

**July 2026 Monetary Policy Report** likewise states: "Inflation remains elevated relative to the Committee's 2 percent goal, in part reflecting supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy. The Committee will deliver price stability." [D17][D22] It adds that over the 12 months ending May, total PCE rose 4.1% and core PCE 3.4%, driven by earlier tariff hikes, an energy-price surge from the Middle East conflict, and AI-related demand [D14][D15]. The report's June 2026 SEP shows median PCE inflation of 3.6% (2026), 2.3% (2027), 2.0% (2028), and core PCE of 3.3% (2026), 2.5% (2027) [D11].

## Policy context

The Fed's response to the re-acceleration was to hike: the Committee decided on September 16, 2026, to raise the target range by 25 basis points, with the change effective September 17, 2026, moving the range from 3.50%–3.75% to 3.75%–4.00% [D3][M1][M2]. This follows a period of cuts in late 2025 (the range had been lowered to 3.50%–3.75% by December 11, 2025) [M1][M2].

**Bottom line:** Inflation is not coming down on the measures the Fed prioritizes. Headline and core PCE re-accelerated to multi-year highs in May 2026 and, while easing slightly since, remain well above 2%, prompting the Committee to hike in September and to describe inflation as "elevated" and "too high." Only core CPI is on a clear downward trend.

One caveat: the MPR's dedicated staff baseline inflation forecast (as distinct from the participant SEP medians) was not available in the material reviewed, so the numeric outlook above reflects the Committee's Summary of Economic Projections rather than the staff's separate projection.

Taking "is inflation coming down?" to mean the current trend in U.S. headline and core CPI/PCE over the last several months, and the "latest Fed view" to mean the September 15–16, 2026 FOMC meeting and the July 2026 Monetary Policy Report: **No — by the Fed's preferred measures, inflation is not coming down; it re-accelerated sharply in spring 2026 and remains well above the 2% goal, which is why the Committee hiked rates on September 16, 2026.** The one bright spot is core CPI, which has been falling steadily.

## What the data show (latest readings: August 2026)

Headline and core PCE — the measures the Fed emphasizes — are still elevated and only modestly off their spring peaks:

| Measure (YoY) | Jun 2025 | Peak (May 2026) | Latest (Aug 2026) | Trend |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Headline CPI | 2.68% | 4.17% | 3.35% | Up, then partial pullback [M4] |
| Headline PCE | 2.61% | 3.82% | 3.42% | Up, then partial pullback [M3] |
| Core PCE (Fed's preferred) | 2.83% | 3.16% | 3.01% | Up, then partial pullback [M5] |
| Core CPI | 2.91% | 3.11% (Aug 2025) | 2.45% | Steadily down, 15-month low [M6] |

So the picture is mixed: headline and core PCE spiked from mid-2025 to a May 2026 high and have eased somewhat over the last three months, but they remain far above 2%. Core CPI is the exception, declining from 3.11% (Aug 2025) to 2.45% (Aug 2026) [M6]. Month-over-month, headline measures jumped in Feb–Mar 2026 (CPI +0.87%/+0.64%; PCE +0.63%/+0.44%), turned negative in June (CPI −0.42%; PCE −0.10%), and ticked back up in July–August [M7][M8]. Note the latest available data is for August 2026; September 2026 readings are not yet out (expected mid-October 2026).

## What the latest Fed documents say

**September 16, 2026 FOMC statement** (12–0 vote, a 25 bp hike to 3¾–4%): "Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability." [D3] Notably, the statement does *not* use the softer "moving toward 2 percent" or "disinflationary progress" language — the framing is "elevated" plus a commitment to a "timelier return."

**Chair Warsh's press conference (Sept 16, 2026)** was more emphatic: "inflation is too high and has been for too long," and "This summer's inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved." He cited total PCE around 3.6% in August, core PCE about 3.2%, and CPI about 2.4%, with "too many categories" still rising above 3% on 6- and 12-month bases [D5]. He said the standard for easing — being "confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed" — "has not been satisfied" [D6]. On the Summary of Economic Projections, he noted median total PCE inflation of 3.7% this year falling to 2.3% next year, with "inflation risks to the upside" [D6]. When asked how a "timelier return" squares with the median pushing 2% out to 2029, Warsh stressed those were his colleagues' forecasts, not his own, and reaffirmed the commitment to deliver price stability [D10].

**July 2026 Monetary Policy Report** likewise states: "Inflation remains elevated relative to the Committee's 2 percent goal, in part reflecting supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy. The Committee will deliver price stability." [D17][D22] It adds that over the 12 months ending May, total PCE rose 4.1% and core PCE 3.4%, driven by earlier tariff hikes, an energy-price surge from the Middle East conflict, and AI-related demand [D14][D15]. The report's June 2026 SEP shows median PCE inflation of 3.6% (2026), 2.3% (2027), 2.0% (2028), and core PCE of 3.3% (2026), 2.5% (2027) [D11].

## Policy context

The Fed's response to the re-acceleration was to hike: the target range is now 3.75%–4.00% as of October 5, 2026, after a 25 bp increase on September 17, 2026 (from 3.50%–3.75%) [M1][M2]. This follows a period of cuts in late 2025 (the range had been lowered to 3.50%–3.75% by December 11, 2025) [M1][M2].

**Bottom line:** Inflation is not coming down on the measures the Fed prioritizes. Headline and core PCE re-accelerated to multi-year highs in May 2026 and, while easing slightly since, remain well above 2%, prompting the Committee to hike in September and to describe inflation as "elevated" and "too high." Only core CPI is on a clear downward trend.

One caveat: the MPR's dedicated staff baseline inflation forecast (as distinct from the participant SEP medians) was not available in the material reviewed, so the numeric outlook above reflects the Committee's Summary of Economic Projections rather than the staff's separate projection.

question: What are the Federal Reserve's main concerns about the economy right now?
answer:
Taking "right now" to mean the most recent documents in the collection—the September 15–16, 2026 FOMC meeting, the July 2026 Beige Book and Monetary Policy Report, the July 28–29, 2026 minutes, and speeches through October 1, 2026—the Federal Reserve's dominant concern is that **inflation remains elevated and has been running above the 2 percent target for more than five years**, with risks skewed to the upside. The labor market is viewed as stable and "in good shape," and growth is solid (largely AI-investment-driven), so the Committee's "predominant focus" is on the price-stability side of its mandate [D8][D10][D30].

## 1. Inflation: the central concern
- **FOMC statement (Sept 16, 2026):** "Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability." The Committee voted 12–0 to **raise** the federal funds target range by 25 bps to 3¾–4 percent [D8].
- **Chair Warsh (Sept 16 press conference):** "for more than five years, inflation has been running above target. So our predominant focus is on the price-stability side of our mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long." He cited 12-month total PCE likely around 3.6 percent in August, core PCE about 3.2 percent, and CPI about 2.4 percent, noting "too many categories are still posting increases above 3 percent" [D10].
- **Chair Warsh (Jackson Hole, Aug 28, 2026):** 12-month PCE inflation 3.7 percent (six-month 4.1 percent); 54 percent of PCE components rose more than 3 percent over the past year versus 32 percent pre-pandemic; the 2 percent PCE target is "a firm, fixed target," and "price stability is not self-executing, nor is inflation necessarily mean-reverting" [D28][D30].
- **July 2026 Monetary Policy Report:** total PCE inflation 4.1 percent and core PCE 3.4 percent over the 12 months ending May 2026, up substantially from 2.5 percent and 2.8 percent a year earlier, driven by tariffs, the Middle East conflict's energy price surge, and AI-related demand [D34][D58].
- **July 28–29, 2026 minutes:** price increases were "broad based," elevated in core services ex-housing and in underlying inflation; risks to the inflation forecast were "skewed to the upside, with the possibility that inflation would prove to be more persistent than the staff anticipated" [D11][D12].

## 2. Upside inflation risks and persistence
- **Chair Warsh (Sept 16):** "Inflation risks are to the upside while labor risks are roughly balanced." The Committee aims to ensure "relative price changes in some sectors of the economy do not broaden," that "inflation compensation in market prices stays low," and that "inflation expectations remain well anchored" [D9].
- **July minutes:** "Many participants highlighted the possibility that, after several years of inflation above 2 percent, continued elevated inflation rates could begin to affect inflation expectations and wage- and price-setting decisions," and that "successive supply shocks have repeatedly delayed the expected return of inflation to 2 percent" [D12].
- **Governor Barr (Sept 29, 2026):** inflation has exceeded target for five and a half years; "only two months of data consistent with 2 percent core PCE inflation over the past 20 months"; "further policy adjustments are likely to be needed" [D49–D51, D60].
- **Governor Jefferson (Oct 1, 2026):** upside inflation risks from energy (Middle East conflict), the AI buildout, and trade policy; supported the September hike to keep expectations anchored [D52–D54].
- **Governor Cook (Aug 5, 2026):** warned that with five years of above-target inflation, "the risk of entrenched inflation expectations grows" and she was "prepared to act by raising rates, if necessary" [D62–D64].
- **Governor Waller (Sept 3, 2026):** noted "signs of disinflation" (three-month core PCE down from 4.76 percent in February to 3.05 percent) but said he would support a hike "if inflation comes in hot" [D46–D48].

## 3. Geopolitical / supply-shock uncertainty
- **FOMC statement (Sept 16):** "uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments" [D8].
- **July minutes:** "the recent re-escalation of the conflict in the Middle East significantly clouded the inflation outlook," and a protracted conflict "could prolong supply chain challenges and could put upward pressures on inflation" [D12].
- **July 2026 MPR:** energy prices leaped 24 percent over the 12 months ending May 2026 following the start of the Middle East conflict in late February [D58].
- **Beige Book (July 2026):** several Districts tied cost increases to the Middle East conflict or tariffs; Districts flagged "elevated uncertainty in the outlook for fuel costs" and margin compression [D17][D31][D33][D55].

## 4. AI-related economic and financial-stability risks
- **July minutes:** strength in business investment "remained concentrated in AI-related expenditures"; a downside risk was "the possibility that AI developments could disappoint, leading to a significant repricing of stocks, with consequent negative effects on consumer spending." Financial-stability discussion focused on "vulnerabilities associated with the financing of the rapid buildout of AI-related infrastructure," high AI equity valuations, private credit, and Treasury market volatility [D13][D20].
- **Chair Warsh (Jackson Hole):** AI is "a new variable—potentially a new factor of production" with a task force studying it; more than half of this year's cap-ex growth is likely AI-related [D26–D27, D29].
- **Governor Barr (Sept 29):** the AI buildout is "driving chip/equipment price increases and supply constraints" [D49–D51].
- **July 2026 MPR:** financial system "sound and resilient" but with "asset valuations above historical norms," elevated hedge fund/life insurer leverage, and some private credit vehicles facing notable redemption requests in Q1 2026 [D36].

## 5. Labor market and growth: stable, not the main worry
- **FOMC statement (Sept 16):** "Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace… Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little" [D8].
- **Chair Warsh (Sept 16):** "the jobless rate remains low at around 4.1 percent… the labor side of the Fed's congressional remit is in good shape" [D10].
- **July minutes:** labor market "stable, with labor demand and supply in balance"; a few noted "lingering signs of softness" (low job-finding rate, elevated long-term unemployment) and upside wage risks [D12][D13].
- **July 2026 MPR:** unemployment 4.2 percent in June, "low and little changed since last summer"; labor supply growth slowed due to lower immigration and aging [D35].
- **SEP medians (Sept 2026):** real GDP 2.3 percent (2026) and 2.4 percent (2027); unemployment 4.1 percent through 2029; PCE inflation 3.7 percent (2026) falling to 2.3 percent (2027); median appropriate federal funds rate 4.1 percent at end-2026 and end-2027, declining to 3.9 percent (2028) and 3.6 percent (2029) [D41].

## 6. Strains on households and financial conditions
- **July minutes:** "low- and moderate-income households were under increasing strains, with inflation eroding their real disposable income" [D13].
- **Beige Book (July 2026):** consumer spending "edged up as higher prices, particularly for fuel, dampened sales in other categories," with "trading down to more affordable varieties"; agricultural conditions deteriorated [D17][D31].
- **Chair Warsh (Sept 16):** "I would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive… So we removed a dose of accommodation" [D39].

## 7. Policy stance and forward risk
- **July 28–29, 2026 meeting:** the Committee voted 9–3 to **hold** rates at 3½–3¾ percent; Hammack, Kashkari, and Logan dissented in favor of a 25 bps hike, arguing price pressures were broad based and a more restrictive stance was needed to "forestall the need for a steeper and potentially more costly sequence of tightening moves at a later stage" [D20][D21][D22].
- **September 15–16, 2026 meeting:** the Committee then voted 12–0 to **raise** rates to 3¾–4 percent, with the statement reaffirming that it "will deliver price stability" [D8].

**In short:** across the September 2026 FOMC statement and SEP, the July 2026 Beige Book and Monetary Policy Report, the July 2026 minutes, and speeches through October 1, 2026, the Fed's main concern is persistently elevated inflation (risks to the upside) after more than five years above the 2 percent target, compounded by geopolitical/supply-shock uncertainty, AI-related price and financial-stability vulnerabilities, and strains on lower- and moderate-income households—while the labor market and growth are assessed as solid and stable.

data.text: I have the full "Participants' Views" section (pp. 7–11) and the policy action. Let me submit the findings.

data.answer: At the July 28–29, 2026 FOMC meeting, participants judged that economic activity had continued to expand at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty, supported by strong business investment (concentrated in AI-related spending) and resilient, recently strengthened consumer spending, with solid real GDP growth expected to continue in the near term [D13]. They assessed labor market conditions as stable, with labor demand and supply in balance, the unemployment rate near its longer-run level, payroll gains strengthening and broadening beyond health care, and moderate nominal wage growth consistent with inflation moving toward 2 percent, though a few noted lingering softness (low job-finding rate, elevated long-term unemployment) and upside wage risks [D12][D13]. On inflation, participants acknowledged it remained elevated: total PCE inflation fell in June largely on a sharp drop in energy prices and core inflation edged down, but price increases were broad based, elevated in core services ex-housing and in underlying inflation, with data-center materials (chips, steel) and consumer items (smartphones, computers, software, electricity) under price pressure; most expected inflation to step down as tariff and energy effects wane, but many flagged the risk of more persistently elevated inflation, with risks skewed to the upside, and the re-escalated Middle East conflict significantly clouding the outlook [D11][D12]. Main concerns included: (1) inflation persistence after years above 2 percent, successive supply shocks, and the risk that elevated inflation could feed into expectations and wage/price-setting; (2) AI-related uncertainty—both upside price effects from AI-driven demand and downside risk that AI disappointment could trigger a stock repricing that hits consumer spending, plus financial-stability vulnerabilities in AI infrastructure financing, high AI equity valuations, private credit, and Treasury market volatility; (3) strains on low- and moderate-income households from inflation eroding real disposable income [D11][D12][D13][D20]. On policy, most participants supported maintaining the target range (3½–3¾ percent), reasoning that intermeeting data would reduce uncertainty about inflation; several favored a 25 bps increase, arguing price pressures were broad based and a more restrictive stance was needed, and that acting now could forestall a steeper, costlier tightening later; many assessed tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline, and some said financial conditions were not yet sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation back to 2 percent [D20][D21]. The Committee voted 9–3 to hold rates, with Hammack, Kashkari, and Logan dissenting in favor of a 25 bps hike, and retained the statement language that the Committee "will deliver price stability" [D21][D22].

data.answer:
At the September 15–16, 2026 FOMC meeting, the Committee voted 12–0 to RAISE the federal funds target range by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves [D8]. The statement assessed the economy as strong: "Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little" [D8]. The dominant concern was inflation: "Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability" [D8].

Chair Warsh's press conference elaborated: the labor market is "in good shape" (unemployment ~4.1%, job openings and hours rising, claims consistent with full employment), but "for more than five years, inflation has been running above target... The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long," with total PCE likely ~3.6% in August, core PCE ~3.2%, and CPI ~2.4% [D10]. He framed the hike as removing "a dose of accommodation" because financial conditions were not restrictive, and stated the Committee's standard for action had not been satisfied [D9][D39]. The main risks highlighted were upside inflation risks (labor risks "roughly balanced"), elevated geopolitical uncertainty, and the need to keep inflation expectations well anchored and prevent relative price changes from broadening [D9].

The SEP medians (18 participants) showed real GDP growth of 2.3% (2026) and 2.4% (2027), PCE inflation of 3.7% (2026) falling to 2.3% (2027), core PCE of 3.4% (2026) and 2.5% (2027), unemployment at 4.1% through 2029, and a median appropriate federal funds rate of 4.1% at end-2026 and end-2027, declining to 3.9% (2028) and 3.6% (2029) [D41].
key_facts: FOMC statement (12–0 vote): 'The Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.' [D8]

Statement economic assessment: 'Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.' [D8]
Statement on inflation: 'Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.' [D8]

Chair Warsh: 'the jobless rate remains low at around 4.1 percent, and both job openings and weekly hours have been increasing... So the labor side of the Fed's congressional remit is in good shape.' [D10]

Chair Warsh: 'for more than five years, inflation has been running above target. So our predominant focus is on the price-stability side of our mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long.' [D10]

Chair Warsh on current inflation: 'the 12-month change in total PCE prices likely was around 3.6 percent in August. Core PCE and CPI prices are running at about 3.2 and 2.4 percent, respectively. Too many categories are still posting increases above 3 percent on both a 6- and 12-month basis.' [D10]
Chair Warsh on rationale: 'I would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive. This view was widely shared by the Committee. So we removed a dose of accommodation.' [D39]
Chair Warsh on risks: 'Inflation risks are to the upside while labor risks are roughly balanced.' [D9]

Chair Warsh on objectives: 'We aim to ensure that credit and financial conditions are consistent over time with our mandate, that relative price changes in some sectors of the economy do not broaden, that inflation compensation in market prices stays low, and that inflation expectations remain well anchored.' [D9]
SEP note: 18 participants submitted projections for the September 15–16, 2026 meeting; one did not submit 2028 and 2029 projections. [D42]
Chair Warsh noted he did not offer his own projection, as in June: 'It reflects the views of my colleagues on the Committee, but, as in June, I have not offered a projection of my own.' [D9]

data.answer: Across 2026 speeches, Fed officials share a common core concern: inflation has run above the 2 percent target for more than five years and remains the dominant policy problem, even though the labor market is stable and growth is solid (largely AI-investment-driven). Chairman Kevin Warsh's August 28, 2026 Jackson Hole speech, "In Our Time," delivered on his 100th day as Chair, argued the Fed's "predominant focus right now should be on prices": 12-month PCE inflation was 3.7 percent (six-month 4.1 percent), progress over two years has been "modest," and 54 percent of PCE components rose more than 3 percent over the past year versus 32 percent pre-pandemic. He stressed that the 2 percent PCE target is a "firm, fixed target," that inflation is not self-correcting, that the Fed bears responsibility for "65 months of sustained, elevated inflation," and that it must be "confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed"—committing to "a discipline, not to a decision" [D25-D30, D44]. He also flagged AI as a new factor of production requiring study, criticized routine forward guidance as having "overstayed its welcome," and warned of a "hall-of-mirrors" problem if markets trade mainly on Fed signals [D26-D27]. Governors echoed the inflation concern: Barr (Sept 29) said inflation has exceeded target for five and a half years, only two months in 20 were consistent with 2 percent core PCE, and the FOMC's unanimous September 25bp hike to 3.75-4.00 percent was needed because inflation risks rose while labor-market risks receded, with further tightening likely [D49-D60]. Jefferson (Oct 1) saw upside inflation risks from energy, the AI buildout, and trade policy, and supported the September hike to anchor expectations [D52-D54]. Waller (Sept 3) noted signs of disinflation (three-month core PCE down from 4.76 percent in February to 3.05 percent) but said he would support a hike if August data showed progress was fleeting [D46-D48]. Cook (Aug 5) warned that with five years of above-target inflation, the risk of entrenched inflation expectations grows and she was "prepared to act by raising rates, if necessary" [D62-D64].
key_facts: Warsh (Jackson Hole, Aug 28, 2026): 12-month PCE inflation 3.7%, six-month 4.1%; 'the Fed's predominant focus right now should be on prices'; 54% of PCE components up >3% over 12 months vs 32% pre-pandemic; 'responsibility for 65 months of sustained, elevated inflation sits squarely with the central bank' [D30].

Warsh: 2% PCE target is 'a firm, fixed target'; 'price stability is not self-executing, nor is inflation necessarily mean-reverting'; standard is being 'confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed'; 'committed to a discipline, not to a decision' [D28, D44].

Warsh: forward guidance 'has overstayed its welcome' in normal times; warned of a 'hall-of-mirrors problem' if markets rely on Fed guidance and the Fed on market prices; AI is 'a new variable—potentially a new factor of production' with a task force studying it [D26-D27].
Warsh: economy resilient—capex up ~9% (highest since 2021, >half AI-related), S&P 500 profits +20%, unemployment 4.1%, but 'credit and loan markets are showing few signs of policy restraint' [D29].

Barr (Detroit, Sept 29, 2026): inflation above target five and a half years; 'only two months of data consistent with 2 percent core PCE inflation over the past 20 months'; FOMC unanimously raised rates 25bp in September; 'further policy adjustments are likely to be needed'; AI buildout driving chip/equipment price increases and supply constraints [D49-D51, D60].

Jefferson (UVA, Oct 1, 2026): 'inflation is too high and has exceeded the Federal Reserve's 2 percent target for more than five years'; 12-month PCE 3.4% in August; upside inflation risks from energy (Middle East conflict), AI buildout, trade policy; supported the September hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent to keep expectations anchored [D52-D54].

Waller (Reuters, Sept 3, 2026): inflation 'meaningfully above' goal but 'finally seeing some signs of disinflation'—three-month core PCE fell from 4.76% (Feb) to 3.05% (Jul); would support holding rates if disinflation continues, but 'if inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike' [D46-D48].

Cook (Anchorage, Aug 5, 2026): 'Inflation is too high'; PCE +3.7% over 12 months through June; risks shifted 'toward inflation and away from the labor market'; 'prepared to act by raising rates, if necessary'; warned of entrenchment risk after five years above target [D62-D64].

data.answer:
The July 2026 Beige Book (2026-07-15) and the July 2026 Monetary Policy Report (2026-07-10) paint a consistent picture: the economy is expanding at a solid pace, but inflation has risen well above the 2% goal, driven by supply shocks (tariffs, the Middle East conflict's energy price surge, and AI-related demand), while the labor market has stabilized after a period of cooling.

Inflation: The MPR reports total PCE inflation of 4.1% and core PCE of 3.4% over the 12 months ending May 2026, up substantially from 2.5% and 2.8% a year earlier [D34][D58]. Drivers include earlier tariff hikes, the energy price surge after the Middle East conflict began in late February, and AI-related demand for high-tech products; short-term inflation expectations moved higher, but long-term expectations remain anchored near 2% [D35]. The Beige Book reports prices increased moderately in nine Districts, robustly in two, and slightly in one, with price growth the same or slower than the prior period in all Districts; non-labor input costs rose (energy, transportation, raw materials), some contacts tied cost increases to the Middle East conflict or tariffs, and a couple of Districts saw selling prices lag input costs, crimping margins [D18][D32].

Labor market: The MPR says the labor market has stabilized with demand and supply roughly in balance — unemployment at 4.2% in June, low and little changed since last summer; subdued layoffs, flat vacancies, but private payroll gains picking up; labor supply growth slowed due to lower immigration and aging [D35]. The Beige Book reports employment rose on balance (five Districts with modest-to-solid gains, seven with little/no change), wage growth modest to moderate, skilled workers hard to find, and some firms using AI in hiring/screening [D31][D32].

Business activity: The Beige Book reports activity increased at a slight-to-moderate pace in 11 of 12 Districts; consumer spending edged up but was dampened by higher fuel prices, with trading down and softer discretionary spending; tourism up (World Cup boost); agriculture deteriorated (lower commodity prices, higher input costs, tighter credit); manufacturing grew modestly-to-moderately led by data center, machinery, and defense orders, with more common supply chain issues; construction/real estate up slightly (data center building); financial conditions stable on net, loan volumes up modestly, consumer loan quality ticked down [D17][D31]. The MPR adds Q1 real GDP growth of 2.1%, robust high-tech business investment, modest household consumption (1.3% annualized through May), stagnant housing, and strong manufacturing output [D35].

Risks/vulnerabilities: The MPR notes elevated uncertainty from the Middle East conflict; financial system sound and resilient with vulnerabilities roughly unchanged, but asset valuations above historical norms, elevated hedge fund/life insurer leverage, and some private credit vehicles facing notable redemption requests in Q1 2026 [D36]. Foreign growth was subdued with foreign inflation rising on energy/commodity prices, prompting several foreign central banks to raise rates [D57]. The FOMC held the federal funds rate at 3½–3¾% since the start of 2026 and emphasized its commitment to delivering price stability at the June meeting [D34][D36]. question: How has Fed monetary policy evolved since 2023?
answer:
Taking "since 2023" to mean from early 2023 through the most recent documents in the collection (the September 16, 2026 FOMC meeting), the Federal Reserve's monetary policy moved through four distinct phases: a final hiking phase in 2023, a long restrictive hold at the 5¼–5½% peak (July 2023–July 2024), a cutting phase (September 2024–December 2025) that brought the federal funds target range to 3½–3¾%, and a 2026 pause that ended with a return to hiking in September 2026 (+25bp to 3¾–4%). Balance-sheet policy (quantitative tightening) ran from June 2022, was slowed twice (June 2024, April 2025), was concluded on December 1, 2025, and was replaced in 2026 by an explicit "ample reserves" management policy. The FOMC's stated rationale shifted from a one-sided inflation fight (2023) to a balanced dual-mandate framing (2024–2025), and back to a firm "deliver price stability" commitment in 2026 as inflation re-accelerated on supply shocks.

## Interest-rate decisions (federal funds target range)

| Period | Action | Range | Stated rationale / key language |
|---|---|---|---|
| Feb 2023 | +25bp | 4½–4¾% | "ongoing increases... appropriate"; "strongly committed to returning inflation to 2 percent" [D132] |
| Mar 2023 | +25bp | 4¾–5% | "some additional policy firming may be appropriate" [D45] |
| May 2023 | +25bp | 5–5¼% | "highly attentive to inflation risks" [D186] |
| Jul 2023 | +25bp | 5¼–5½% (peak) | "strongly committed to returning inflation to 2 percent" [D138] |
| Sep–Dec 2023 | Hold | 5¼–5½% | "highly attentive to inflation risks"; "strongly committed" [D187][D188][D144] |
| Jan–Jul 2024 | Hold | 5¼–5½% | "does not expect it will be appropriate to reduce the target range until [the Committee] has gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent" [D53][D54][D51][D56][D58] |
| Sep 2024 | −50bp | 4¾–5% | "recalibration... toward a more neutral stance"; "risks... roughly in balance" [D60][D97] |
| Nov 2024 | −25bp | 4½–4¾% | "further recalibration" [D218] |
| Dec 2024 | −25bp | 4¼–4½% | "risks... roughly in balance"; "attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate" [D216] |
| Jan–Jul 2025 | Hold | 4¼–4½% | Tariff uncertainty; "well positioned to wait for more clarity" [D111][D172] |
| Sep 2025 | −25bp | 4–4¼% | "downside risks to employment had risen" [D169] |
| Oct 2025 | −25bp | 3¾–4% | Rising employment downside risks [D190] |
| Dec 2025 | −25bp | 3½–3¾% | "downside risks to employment had risen in recent months" [D171] |
| Jan–Jul 2026 | Hold | 3½–3¾% | "attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate" [D210][D211] |
| Sep 2026 | +25bp | 3¾–4% | "will deliver price stability" [D83][D233] |

The March 2024 minutes mark the explicit turning point from hikes to eventual cuts: "participants judged that the policy rate was likely at its peak for this tightening cycle" [D96]. The September 2023 minutes record the last meeting where a hike was still the modal view ("A majority of participants judged that one more increase... would likely be appropriate") [D84]. The first cut in September 2024 was approved with one hawkish dissent: a member voted against the 50bp cut, preferring to lower the target range only to 5–5¼% (i.e., a 25bp cut) [D97][D174].

## Balance-sheet policy (QT → ample reserves)

- 2023: QT ran at $60bn/month Treasury cap and $35bn/month agency/MBS cap; holdings fell ~$500bn to ~$8tn (31% of GDP) [D116][D165][D166].
- June 1, 2024: Treasury cap cut to $25bn/month (agency held at $35bn); excess agency principal reinvested into Treasuries; holdings ~$6.8tn (24% of GDP) [D51][D183][D121].
- April 1, 2025: Treasury cap cut further to $5bn/month (agency held at $35bn); holdings ~$6.5tn (22% of GDP) [D125][D157].
- October 2025: FOMC decided to "conclude the reduction of its aggregate securities holdings on December 1" [D190].
- December 2025: statement said reserve balances had "declined to ample levels" and the Committee "will initiate purchases of shorter-term Treasury securities as needed to maintain an ample supply of reserves" [D191].
- 2026: balance-sheet language replaced by an ample-reserves commitment — "reaffirmed its policy of maintaining ample reserves" (June 2026) [D46] and "continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves" (July and September 2026) [D82][D83]; the balance sheet "ticked up" in 2026 [D128].

## FOMC rationale and outlook (statements, minutes, Monetary Policy Reports)

- 2023 (one-sided inflation fight): statements repeatedly said the Committee was "highly attentive to inflation risks" and "strongly committed to returning inflation to 2 percent" [D132][D138][D187][D188][D144]. The March 2023 Monetary Policy Report judged inflation "well above" 2% (PCE 5.4% in January; core 4.7%) and the labor market "extremely tight," and that returning inflation to 2% "will likely require a period of below-trend growth and some softening of labor market conditions" [D116].
- 2024 (balanced dual mandate): the July 2024 report noted inflation had "eased notably" (PCE 2.6% in May, down from a 7.1% peak) and the labor market had "moved into better balance"; the Committee judged "risks... have moved toward better balance" but "remains highly attentive to inflation risks" [D119][D121]. The September 2024 statement introduced the "greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent" and "risks... roughly in balance" framing [D60].
- 2025 (tariff uncertainty, then employment downside): the February 2025 report described inflation as having "moderated a little further" (PCE 2.6% in December; core 2.8%) and the labor market as having "stabilized... no longer appears especially tight" [D122]. The June 2025 report noted inflation had "continued to moderate" (PCE 2.1% in April; core 2.5%) but was "bumpy," with sentiment declining amid tariff concerns; the Committee was "well positioned to wait for more clarity" [D125]. The June 2025 minutes recorded that "some participants saw the most likely appropriate path... as involving no reductions... this year" citing tariff-driven upside inflation risks [D111]. By September–December 2025 the minutes emphasized that "downside risks to employment had risen" [D169][D171]. The December 2025 press conference characterized inflation risks as "tilted to the upside and risks to employment to the downside," with tariffs seen as "relatively short lived—a one-time shift in the price level" [D151].
- 2026 (supply-driven inflation re-acceleration, firmer price-stability language): the July 2026 report found inflation had "risen this year and remains elevated" (PCE 4.1% in May; core 3.4%), driven by supply shocks (tariffs, Middle East conflict energy surge, AI demand), with the labor market "broadly stable"; the FOMC "emphasized its commitment to delivering price stability" [D128][D129][D130]. The 2026 statements dropped the "somewhat elevated" qualifier and the "balance of risks" language, adopting a firmer "The Committee will deliver price stability" commitment [D83][D229]. The September 2026 press conference (Chair Warsh) stated: "Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. This Committee will deliver price stability" [D229].

## Committee projections (SEP dot plots)

From the stacked SEP Table 1 (median projections, all 15 releases March 22, 2023–September 16, 2026) [D185]:
- Longer-run federal funds rate median rose from 2.5% (March 2023) to 3.2% (September 2026).
- The 2026 median federal funds rate rose from 3.4% (March 2025) to 3.8% (June 2026) to 4.1% (September 2026); the 2027 median rose from 3.1% to 3.6% to 4.1%, implying the Committee now expects the policy rate to stay near 4% through 2027 before easing to 3.9%

data.text: I now have comprehensive coverage of all five reports. Let me compile the findings.

data.answer: Across the five Monetary Policy Reports, the staff's assessment shifted from a "too hot" economy (2023) through a rebalancing (2024), to a stabilized economy with bumpy disinflation (early 2025), to a solid but tariff-uncertain economy (mid-2025), and finally to a solidly growing economy with renewed, supply-driven inflation (2026). Inflation risks moved from clearly weighted to the upside (2023) to "better balance" (mid-2024), to attention to both sides of the dual mandate (early 2025), to a wait-and-see posture amid tariff uncertainty (mid-2025), and back to a firm emphasis on delivering price stability (2026). On the policy framework, the 2019-20 framework (2% inflation goal, average-inflation targeting) was reaffirmed throughout, but a new periodic framework review began in 2025 (explicitly not targeting the 2% goal) and by 2026 had evolved into independent task forces examining communications, balance-sheet policy, data, productivity, and inflation drivers. On balance-sheet policy (QT), the Fed ran predictable runoff from June 2022, slowed the Treasury cap in June 2024, slowed it again in April 2025, and by December 2025 judged reserves had reached ample levels and switched from runoff to reserve-management purchases of short-term Treasuries, with the balance sheet ticking up in 2026.
key_facts: March 2023: Inflation 'well above' 2% (PCE 5.4% in Jan; core 4.7%); labor market 'extremely tight'; staff judged returning inflation to 2% 'will likely require a period of below-trend growth and some softening of labor market conditions'; FOMC raised the funds rate 3pp since June to 4½-4¾% and 'anticipates ongoing increases'; QT caps $60bn/mo Treasuries, $35bn/mo agency, holdings down ~$500bn to ~$8tn (31% of GDP). [D116][D118][D165][D166]

July 2024: Inflation 'eased notably' (PCE 2.6% in May, down from 7.1% peak); labor market 'moved into better balance'; Committee judged 'risks to achieving its employment and inflation goals have moved toward better balance' but 'remains highly attentive to inflation risks'; funds rate held at 5¼-5½% since July 2023; QT slowed June 1, 2024 (Treasury cap cut to $25bn/mo), holdings down ~$1.7tn to ~$6.8tn (24% of GDP). [D119][D121][D183]

February 2025: Inflation 'moderated a little further' (PCE 2.6% in Dec; core 2.8%); labor market 'stabilized... no longer appears especially tight'; FOMC cut 100bp over Sep/Nov/Dec 2024 to 4¼-4½%, citing 'greater confidence in inflation moving sustainably toward 2 percent'; QT at $25bn/$35bn caps, holdings down ~$2tn to ~$6.5tn (22% of GDP); a public review of the monetary policy framework began (2% goal 'not a focus of the review'). [D122][D124][D156][D157][D184]

June 2025: Inflation 'continued to moderate' (PCE 2.1% in Apr; core 2.5%) but 'bumpy'; labor market 'in solid shape'; GDP 'paused' in Q1; sentiment declined amid tariff concerns; FOMC held at 4¼-4½%, 'well positioned to wait for more clarity'; QT further slowed April 1, 2025 (Treasury cap cut to $5bn/mo, agency held at $35bn); framework review ongoing, to conclude by late summer. [D125][D126][D159][D160][D161]

July 2026: Inflation 'risen this year and remains elevated' (PCE 4.1% in May; core 3.4%), driven by supply shocks (tariffs, Middle East conflict energy surge, AI demand); labor market 'broadly stable'; FOMC held at 3½-3¾% and 'emphasized its commitment to delivering price stability'; at Dec 2025 meeting FOMC judged reserves had declined to ample levels and initiated reserve-management purchases of short-term Treasuries (reaffirmed June 2026), so the balance sheet 'ticked up'; five independent task forces launched to review communications, balance-sheet policy, data, productivity/jobs, and inflation drivers. [D128][D129][D130][D162][D163][D164]
data.gaps: The reports describe the Committee's own risk language and staff projections in the SEP section; I did not extract the precise staff median forecast numbers (GDP/inflation/unemployment) from each SEP table, which would require reading the data tables. The 2026 task-force details (five areas) are from the July 2026 report's summary; the 2025 framework review's eventual conclusions are not in this collection's reports (review was to conclude late summer 2025).

data.answer: From the stacked SEP Table 1 (median projections, all 15 releases from March 22, 2023 through September 16, 2026) [D185]: the Committee's terminal federal funds rate (median, "Longer run") rose from 2.5% in March 2023 to 3.2% by September 2026, and the dot plot shifted sharply upward in 2025-2026: the 2026 median went from 3.4% (March 2025) to 3.8% (June 2026) to 4.1% (September 2026), and the 2027 median from 3.1% to 3.6% to 4.1%, implying the Committee now expects the policy rate to stay near 4% through 2027 before easing to 3.9% (2028) and 3.6% (2029). Inflation expectations also moved up: the 2026 PCE median rose from 2.2% (March 2025) to 3.7% (September 2026), and core PCE from 2.2% to 3.4%, while the 2025 PCE median peaked at 3.0% (June/September 2025) before easing to 2.9% (December 2025). Unemployment projections stayed in a narrow 4.1-4.5% band throughout, drifting down to 4.1% by 2026-2029.

data.text: I now have a comprehensive picture of the full arc from 2023 through July 2026, including the key turning points and dissents. Let me submit my findings.

data.answer: Across the FOMC minutes from 2023 through July 2026, participants' deliberations moved through four distinct phases. (1) 2023 was dominated by the question of whether to keep hiking: inflation was "well above" 2 percent and the labor market "very tight," so a majority still saw one more hike as likely appropriate (June–September 2023), before the Committee settled into a restrictive hold at 5¼–5½ percent by December 2023. (2) The pivotal turn from hikes to cuts came in 2024: by March 2024 participants judged the rate "likely at its peak," and after two more holds (June, July) the Committee cut 50 bps in September 2024, then 25 bps in November and December, reaching 4¼–4½ percent. (3) In 2025 the tariff shock reversed the easing momentum: the Committee held at 4¼–4½ percent from January through July as participants flagged upside inflation risks from tariffs, then resumed cutting in September (25 bps to 4–4¼), October (to 3¾–4), and December (to 3½–3¾), each time citing rising downside risks to employment. (4) In 2026 the debate flipped again toward the possibility of hikes: with inflation "elevated" (partly from energy/Middle East supply shocks) and the labor market stabilizing, the Committee held at 3½–3¾ percent at every meeting, and by June–July 2026 a few participants argued there was a case for raising the rate. Notable dissents: September 2024 (one member wanted a smaller 25 bp cut), December 2024 (one member wanted to hold), September 2025 (one member wanted a 50 bp cut), December 2025 (three members dissented — two to hold, one for a 50 bp cut), and March/April 2026 (one member each wanted a 25 bp cut); the most striking was July 2026, when the hold was approved 9–3 with three members (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) voting to raise the rate.
key_facts: 2023-09-20: 'A majority of participants judged that one more increase in the target federal funds rate at a future meeting would likely be appropriate, while some judged it likely that no further increases would be warranted' — the last meeting where a hike was the modal view [D84].
2023-12-13: 'all participants judged it appropriate to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 5¼ to 5½ percent' — restrictive hold, inflation 'eased... but remained elevated' [D88].
2024-03-20: 'participants judged that the policy rate was likely at its peak for this tightening cycle' — the explicit turning point from hikes to eventual cuts [D96].

2024-09-18: 'a substantial majority of participants supported lowering the target range... by 50 basis points to 4¾ to 5 percent'; 'One member voted against that decision, preferring to lower the target range... to 5 to 5¼ percent' — first cut, with a hawkish dissent [D97][D174].
2024-11-07: 'all participants viewed it as appropriate to lower the target range... by 25 basis points to 4½ to 4¾ percent' [D218].
2024-12-18: 'One member voted against that decision, preferring to maintain the target range... at 4½ to 4¾ percent' — cut to 4¼–4½, with a hold dissent [D216].

2025-06-18: 'Some participants saw the most likely appropriate path of monetary policy as involving no reductions in the target range... this year' citing tariff-driven upside inflation risks; all held at 4¼–4½ [D111][D172].

2025-09-17: 'almost all members agreed to lower the target range... ¼ percentage point to 4 to 4¼ percent. One member voted against that decision, preferring to lower the target range ½ percentage point' — easing resumed on rising employment downside risks [D169].

2025-12-10: 'nine members agreed to lower the target range... by ¼ percentage point to 3½ to 3¾ percent. Three members voted against that decision; two preferred to leave the target range unchanged, while the other preferred to lower the target range ½ percentage point' [D171].
2026-01-28 and 2026-03-18: held at 3½–3¾; at both, 'One member voted against that decision and preferred to lower the target range ¼ percentage point' [D210][D211].

2026-06-17: 'A few participants commented that... there was a case for raising the target range for the federal funds rate, but those participants indicated that they supported maintaining the current target range'; hold approved 12–0 [D100][D179].

2026-07-29: hold at 3½–3¾ approved by a 9–3 vote; 'Voting against this action: Beth M. Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie K. Logan, who preferred to raise the target range... by ¼ percentage point' — the first recorded dissent favoring a hike [D178][D222].
2026-04-29: 'The vast majority of participants noted an increased risk that inflation would take longer to return to the Committee's 2 percent objective'; one member wanted a 25 bp cut [D107][D209].
data.gaps: I did not read every one of the 31 minutes in full; the arc is reconstructed from the policy-outlook and Committee Policy Actions sections of each meeting, which is where the rate-path views and votes are recorded. I did not independently verify the identity of each dissenting member for the 2024 and 2025 meetings (the minutes name only the July 2026 dissenters explicitly in the passages retrieved). The 2026-07-29 minutes also note Kevin Warsh as Chairman, reflecting a 2026 leadership change I did not separately research.

data.text: I now have a complete, verified picture of all FOMC statements and press conferences from 2023 through September 2026. Let me compile the findings.

data.answer:
From February 2023 through September 2026 the federal funds target range moved through four distinct phases: (1) a final hiking phase in 2023, (2) a long holding phase at the 5¼–5½% peak (Sep 2023–Jul 2024), (3) a cutting phase (Sep 2024–Dec 2025) that brought the range to 3½–3¾%, and (4) a 2026 pause followed by a return to hiking (Sep 2026, +25bp to 3¾–4%). In 2023 the Committee raised the range to 4½–4¾% (Feb), 4¾–5% (Mar), and 5–5¼% (May) [D132][D45][D186], then held at 5¼–5½% from July through December 2023 [D138][D187][D188][D144], citing restrictive policy, cumulative tightening, and "highly attentive to inflation risks." In 2024 it held at 5¼–5½% through July [D53][D54][D51][D56][D58], then cut 50bp to 4¾–5% in September [D60], 25bp to 4½–4¾% in November [D62], and 25bp to 4¼–4½% in December [D64], framing the cuts as a "recalibration" toward a more neutral stance. In 2025 it held at 4¼–4½% through July (tariff uncertainty) [D52][D66][D67][D69][D70], then cut 25bp each in September (to 4–4¼%), October (to 3¾–4%), and December (to 3½–3¾%) as downside employment risks rose [D189][D190][D191]. In 2026 it held at 3½–3¾% from January through July [D234][D79][D80][D46][D82], then raised 25bp to 3¾–4% in September [D83][D233].

Rationale evolved from a one-sided inflation fight (2023: "strongly committed to returning inflation to 2 percent," "highly attentive to inflation risks") to a balanced dual-mandate framing (2024–2025: "risks ... roughly in balance," "attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate"), with tariffs (2025) and then Middle East/energy supply shocks (2026) becoming the dominant inflation drivers. The 2026 statements dropped the "somewhat elevated" qualifier and the "balance of risks" language, adopting a firmer "The Committee will deliver price stability" commitment.

Balance-sheet language: 2023–2024 statements said the Committee "will continue reducing its holdings of Treasury securities and agency debt and agency MBS"; in May 2024 the statement specified the $35 billion monthly redemption cap and reinvestment of excess principal into Treasuries [D55]. The Oct 2025 statement announced the decision to "conclude the reduction of its aggregate securities holdings on December 1" [D190], and the Dec 2025 statement said reserve balances had "declined to ample levels" and the Committee "will initiate purchases of shorter-term Treasury securities as needed to maintain an ample supply of reserves" [D191]. From 2026 the balance-sheet language was replaced by an ample-reserves commitment: "reaffirmed its policy of maintaining ample reserves" (Jun 2026) [D46] and "continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves" (Jul and Sep 2026) [D82][D83].

Forward guidance: the 2023 statements used "some additional policy firming may be appropriate" and "sufficiently restrictive" language; 2024 statements dropped the "firming" language and added "does not expect it will be appropriate to reduce the target range until [the Committee] has gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent" [D51]. The 2024 press conferences added "policy rate is likely at its peak" (Mar 2024) [D147] and "not on any preset course" (Sep 2024) [D150]. By 2025–2026 the statements relied on "carefully assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks" with no explicit forward guidance. The FOMC also approved updates to its Statement on Longer-Run Goals (consensus statement) on Aug 22, 2025 [D44][D219] and reaffirmed it Jan 28, 2026 [D77]. Notably, the Chair changed from Powell to Warsh in 2026 (Warsh's first press conference was Jun 17, 2026) [D226][D229].

The June 2023 hold at 5–5¼% is confirmed by the press conference [D196]. I did not independently verify the exact 25bp step for the Sep 2024 50bp cut beyond the press conference text [D150], but the statement and press conference agree on the 4¾–5% level. The 2026 statements (Jun–Sep) no longer include the "balance of risks" or "somewhat elevated" inflation language, which I noted as a qualitative shift but did not exhaustively compare word-for-word across all 2026 statements.

data.answer:
Taking "since 2023" to mean from early 2023 through the most recent documents in the collection (the September 16, 2026 FOMC meeting), the Federal Reserve's monetary policy moved through four distinct phases: a final hiking phase in 2023, a long restrictive hold at the 5¼–5½% peak (July 2023–July 2024), a cutting phase (September 2024–December 2025) that brought the federal funds target range to 3½–3¾%, and a 2026 pause that ended with a return to hiking in September 2026 (+25bp to 3¾–4%). Balance-sheet policy (quantitative tightening) ran from June 2022, was slowed twice (June 2024, April 2025), was concluded on December 1, 2025, and was replaced in 2026 by an explicit "ample reserves" management policy. The FOMC's stated rationale shifted from a one-sided inflation fight (2023) to a balanced dual-mandate framing (2024–2025), and back to a firm "deliver price stability" commitment in 2026 as inflation re-accelerated on supply shocks.

question: What does the Federal Reserve say about artificial intelligence?
answer:
Taking "the Federal Reserve" to mean the official views and statements of Fed officials (Governors, Vice Chairs, the Chair) and Fed research staff as found in the local collection of speeches and notes from 2025–2026: the Fed describes AI as a transformative general-purpose technology that will raise productivity and growth, is actively deploying AI in its own operations (while the FOMC does not use AI to set policy), and is monitoring AI's financial-stability risks—algorithmic trading, cyber, and leveraged AI-infrastructure investment. The most recent and authoritative statements (Governor Lisa D. Cook, September 28, 2026) frame AI investment as a current, net inflationary pressure that will delay disinflation, while earlier 2025 statements (Governors Barr, Jefferson) emphasized AI's ultimately disinflationary productivity gains and counseled humility on the near-term monetary-policy effect.

### Consensus Across Fed Officials

*   **AI as a general-purpose technology.** Governor Cook calls AI "the most significant technological shift of our lifetime," on par with the steam engine, electricity, and the internet, affecting monetary policy, financial stability, supervision, and Fed operations [D1]. Governor Waller (February 24, 2026) calls it a technological revolution unlike any in his lifetime, and the Fed is "no different" in trying to incorporate it [D28].
*   **The Fed uses AI internally; the FOMC does not use AI to set policy.** Cook states clearly that "the Federal Open Market Committee is not using AI in developing or setting policy," but the Fed uses AI for financial-stability analysis and staff tasks (writing, coding, research) [D37][D70]. Waller details a "System-first" approach with a common internal general-purpose AI platform for all Reserve Bank employees, coding assistants for developers, and AI embedded in enterprise workflows; AI use is not optional and baseline literacy is built into performance goals [D28][D29][D31].
*   **Financial-stability risks to monitor.** Officials consistently flag AI-driven algorithmic trading (correlated trading, model collusion, manipulation, concentration), cyber risk from LLMs/agentic AI, and rising debt/leverage to finance AI infrastructure [D36][D37][D10].

### Distinct Perspectives

*   **Near-term inflation effect.** Cook (May 27, 2026, and September 28, 2026) argues AI investment is now a net inflationary pressure—chips, computers, software prices surging; electricity and water up ~5% over the past year; core goods running >3% annual pace—and expects only "modest disinflation within the next few years" from productivity, not in time to offset broadening pressure [D2][D34][D6]. By contrast, Barr (November 11, 2025) and Jefferson (November 21, 2025) frame AI's productivity gains as ultimately disinflationary, with Jefferson saying it is "too soon to tell" for monetary policy and counseling humility [D33][D35].
*   **Labor market.** Cook and Barr stress that AI-related job losses could precede job gains and hit young/entry-level workers; Cook is "highly attentive" to a supply-side skills-mismatch scenario where the Fed would have limited tools [D4][D34]. Jefferson is more balanced, calling the net employment effect "highly uncertain" [D53]. Fed research (Liu & Webber, March 2026) finds no evidence of a reduction in job postings for firms/industries with higher AI adoption, though skill requirements and wage premia are shifting [D39].
*   **Supervision.** Vice Chair Bowman is the most pro-innovation, urging proportionality and a lighter touch for smaller banks, and noting the Fed/OCC/FDIC amended model-risk guidance to exclude generative/agentic AI [D7][D8][D10].
*   **Dot-com comparison.** Jefferson argues the current AI market differs from the late-1990s bubble (established earnings, lower P/E, ~50 publicly traded AI-focused firms vs. 1,000+ dot-coms), though he flags rising AI debt as a watch item [D56].

### Key Statements by Official (Time Order)

| Date | Official | Venue | Core message on AI |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-07-17 | Lisa D. Cook | NBER | AI at an "inflection point," next general-purpose technology; four principles for responsible adoption; FOMC not using AI to set policy; AI likely to boost productivity and reduce inflationary pressures over time but could boost prices in the interim via investment surge [D70][D71][D72][D73][D74] |
| 2025-11-11 | Michael S. Barr | Singapore | Two scenarios (incremental GenAI vs. revolution); 3 in 4 large companies used GenAI in 2024; ~$3 trillion new data-center capacity projected; risks include bias in consumer lending and AI trading causing tacit collusion; Fed has an AI program with a "hands on keys" approach [D48][D49][D50][D51] |
| 2025-11-21 | Philip N. Jefferson | Cleveland | ~55% of working-age adults used generative AI (Aug 2025); net employment effect "highly uncertain"; "too soon to tell" for monetary policy; current AI market differs from dot-com but rising AI debt is a watch item [D53][D54][D55][D56] |
| 2026-02-24 | Christopher J. Waller | Boston | Fed moving to "System-first" AI approach; common internal AI platform; three deployment modes; AI use not optional; cautions AI "can hallucinate" and brings data-protection, model-risk, bias, and resilience risks [D28][D29][D30][D31] |
| 2026-05-01 | Michelle W. Bowman | FSOC | Fed has monitored bank AI use for nearly a decade; with OCC/FDIC amended model-risk guidance to exclude generative/agentic AI; highlights Anthropic's "Mythos" model and its dual-use cyber risk; Secretary Bessent and Chair Powell convened largest banks to discuss Mythos [D9][D10][D11] |
| 2026-05-27 | Lisa D. Cook | Stanford | PCE inflation 3.8% (12 months to April 2026), core 3.3%; >$1.5 trillion in announced data-center plans; risks tilted toward higher inflation, prepared to raise rates if disinflation doesn't resume; financial-stability risks: algorithmic trading, AI-disruption hitting speculative-grade tech bonds and BDC redemptions, rising AI-infrastructure debt, cyber risk; FOMC not using AI to set policy [D33][D34][D35][D36][D37][D38] |
| 2026-07-07 | Michelle W. Bowman | FSB | Chairs FSB Standing Committee on Supervisory and Regulatory Cooperation; FSB "Sound Practices for Responsible Adoption of AI" consultation report to be finalized as a U.S. G-20 deliverable; emphasizes materiality and proportionality—lower-risk AI uses should get a lighter supervisory touch [D7][D8] |
| 2026-09-28 | Lisa D. Cook | Oakland | AI "the most significant technological shift of our lifetime"; AI-driven investment pushed up prices of chips, computers, software; electricity and water up ~5% over the past year; core goods >3% annual pace; expects only "modest disinflation within the next few years"; voted to raise rates 25bp at the September 2026 meeting (total inflation ~3.8%, core ~3.4%); labor market resilient (unemployment 4.1% in Aug 2026) but "highly attentive" to a supply-side skills-mismatch scenario [D1][D2][D3][D4][D5][D6] |

### Fed Research Findings (FEDS Notes, 2025–2026)

*   **Labor market.** Liu & Webber (March 2026): no evidence of a reduction in job postings for industries or firms with higher AI adoption; the post-pandemic slowdown in job postings is not driven by AI [D39]. Tito (September 2026): AI skill requirements in manufacturing job postings surged in H2 2025, reaching 11% of postings (vs. 8% economy-wide), up from ~1% in 2018; AI-skill postings in manufacturing command ~70% higher wages than all manufacturing postings [D47]. Soto, Thieu & Allen (July 2026): early evidence suggests AI is impacting younger workers via slower hiring rather than outright layoffs; programming-intensive occupations (NAICS 54) are most exposed [D19].

data.answer: The collection contains a rich set of FEDS Notes (2025–2026) and two relevant press releases that complement speeches on AI's economic effects. No dedicated AI working papers were found among the 2026 FEDS working papers, but the FEDS Notes provide substantial research findings. Key insights span three areas: (1) labor market impacts — early evidence shows no aggregate job posting reductions from AI adoption, though skill requirements and wage premia are shifting; (2) productivity and investment — the AI buildout is generating an investment boom comparable to the 1990s IT boom, with risks of overinvestment and current account deterioration; and (3) adoption patterns — roughly 18% of firms had adopted AI by end-2025, with significant heterogeneity by size and sector. The Federal Reserve also established a dedicated "Productivity and Jobs" task force (July 2026) to assess AI's economic impact on monetary policy.
key_facts: FEDS Note (Liu & Webber, March 2026): No evidence of a reduction in job postings for industries or firms with higher AI adoption. The post-pandemic slowdown in job postings is not driven by AI. However, results focus on total postings, not specific susceptible occupations. [D39]

FEDS Note (Liu & Webber, March 2026): 45.9% of survey respondents reported LLM adoption at work in June/July 2025, up from 30.1% in December 2024. Eloundou et al. (2024) estimate 80% of U.S. workers are in occupations where at least 10% of tasks could be affected by LLMs. [D12]

FEDS Note (Tito, September 2026): AI skill requirements in manufacturing job postings surged in H2 2025, reaching 11% of postings (vs. 8% economy-wide), up from ~1% in 2018. AI-skill postings in manufacturing command ~70% higher wages than all manufacturing postings; for production workers, the AI wage premium has averaged ~30% since 2023. [D46][D47]

FEDS Note (Soto, Thieu & Allen, July 2026): Organizes AI impact indicators into capabilities/costs, firm investment/adoption, and productivity/labor. Notes that as of 2026, evidence points to an economy 'reorganizing around this new technology, with real effects concentrated on certain areas.' METR task-completion horizons have been doubling roughly every several months. [D42][D43]

FEDS Note (Soto et al., July 2026): Early evidence suggests AI is impacting younger workers via slower hiring rather than outright layoffs. Programming-intensive occupations (NAICS 54) are most exposed and likely to show materialized effects first. [D19]

FEDS Note (Allen, April 2026): About 18% of firms had adopted AI as of year-end 2025 (BTOS). Individual-level GenAI work adoption (RPS) stood at ~41% as of November 2025. The Survey of Business Uncertainty found 78% of the labor force works at firms that have adopted AI. Adoption is highest in professional services and financial sectors. [D58][D60]

FEDS Note (Li, July 2026): Models the AI investment boom as an embodied technology shock. Predicts a major GPT breakthrough can induce a lasting investment boom but may end with overinvestment and capital overhang. Notes the recent IP and equipment investment acceleration relative to GDP is comparable to the 1990s IT boom but starting from a much higher base. [D76][D69]

FEDS Note (Fiori, Lipa & Nuenninghoff, July 2026): The AI investment boom is associated with persistent current account deterioration (~10% below historical average) and rising import prices. ~90% of relevant AI equipment is sourced from East Asia. AI-related input prices (computers, semiconductors) have turned upward since the pandemic, posing greater inflation risk than past technology booms. [D65][D66]

FEDS Note (Haag, October 2025): US retains important advantages in AI infrastructure, compute capacity, and investment conditions. US hosted ~4,049 data centers as of 2024 (vs. EU ~2,250, UK 484, China 379). US accounted for >75% of reported private VC in generative AI startups. [D61][D63][D64]

FEDS Note (Timmerman, February 2025): College majors most affected by generative AI include Mathematics/Computer Science, Political Science/Government, and Accounting. Impact may be more pronounced at Liberal Arts I and Research University I institutions. [D79]

Press Release (May 2026, Economic Well-Being report): One in four workers used generative AI at work in the prior month; 81% of users agreed it saves time. AI users were more likely to say it would improve their careers than to worry about job replacement. Non-users saw fewer potential benefits. [D24]

Press Release (July 2026): Federal Reserve established a 'Productivity and Jobs' task force to 'assess the economic impact of new general-purpose technologies, including artificial intelligence, to inform the Federal Reserve's policy judgments.' Co-led by Marc Andreessen (a16z), Charles I. Jones (Stanford/Anthropic), and Asha Sharma (Microsoft/XBOX). [D88]

FEDS Note literature review (October 2025): Acemoglu (2024) finds modest TFP gains (upper bound 0.66% over 10 years) and GDP effects of 0.93%-1.16% over next 10 years with no substantial negative wage effects. OECD (2025) expects labor productivity gains of 0.2-1.3 percentage points over the next decade. [D18][D23]
Press Release (September 2025): Fed announced a payments innovation conference featuring a panel on 'the intersection of artificial intelligence and payments.' [D81]
