key_facts: Cook (2026-09-28, Oakland): AI is 'the most significant technological shift of our lifetime' and a general-purpose technology on par with the steam engine, electricity, and the internet; it affects monetary policy, financial stability, supervision, and Fed operations [D1].

Cook (2026-09-28): AI-driven investment has pushed up prices of chips, computers, software; electricity and water up ~5% over the past year; core goods running >3% annual pace; she expects only 'modest disinflation within the next few years' from productivity, not in time to offset broadening pressure; she voted to raise rates 25bp at the September 2026 meeting (total inflation ~3.8%, core ~3.4%) [D2][D6].

Cook (2026-09-28): labor market resilient so far (unemployment 4.1% in Aug 2026) but she is 'highly attentive' to a scenario where AI raises unemployment via a supply-side skills mismatch, where the Fed would have limited tools; small firms: nearly half of small employer firms use AI and 71% report increased productivity (Small Business Credit Survey) [D3][D4][D5].

Bowman (2026-07-07, FSB): chairs FSB Standing Committee on Supervisory and Regulatory Cooperation; FSB 'Sound Practices for Responsible Adoption of AI' consultation report to be finalized as a U.S. G-20 deliverable; emphasizes materiality and proportionality—lower-risk AI uses should get a lighter supervisory touch, and guidance must fit smaller institutions [D7][D8].

Bowman (2026-05-01, FSOC): Fed has monitored bank AI use for nearly a decade; with OCC and FDIC the Fed amended model risk management guidance to clarify it does NOT apply to generative or agentic AI (applies narrowly to traditional models and basic AI); highlights Anthropic's 'Mythos' model that detects cyber vulnerabilities—dual-use risk; Secretary Bessent and Chair Powell convened the largest banks to discuss Mythos [D9][D10][D11].

Waller (2026-02-24, Boston): Fed is moving to a 'System-first' approach with shared standards/infrastructure while preserving decentralization for monetary policy and research; built a common internal general-purpose AI platform for all Reserve Bank employees; three deployment modes: general-purpose AI for all staff, coding assistants for developers ('two days now takes two hours'), and AI embedded in enterprise workflows; AI use is not optional—baseline literacy built into performance goals; cautions AI 'can hallucinate' and brings data-protection, model-risk, bias, and resilience risks requiring guardrails, model validation, and human accountability [D28][D29][D30][D31].

Cook (2026-05-27, Stanford): PCE inflation 3.8% (12 months to April 2026), core 3.3%—highest since 2023; >$1.5 trillion in announced data-center plans; risks tilted toward higher inflation, prepared to raise rates if disinflation doesn't resume; financial-stability risks: AI-driven algorithmic trading (correlated trading, model collusion, manipulation, concentration), AI-disruption concerns hitting speculative-grade tech bonds and BDC redemptions, and rising debt/leverage to finance AI infrastructure (hyperscaler IG bond deals, private debt); cyber risk from LLMs/agentic AI (Anthropic Mythos Preview); FOMC is NOT using AI in developing or setting policy, but Fed uses AI for financial-stability analysis (agentic AI sprint, active knowledge distillation cutting compute costs up to 80%, NLP on Beige Book data for recession forecasting) [D33][D34][D35][D36][D37][D38].

Barr (2025-11-11, Singapore): two scenarios—incremental GenAI adoption augmenting tasks vs. a revolution transforming work; 3 in 4 large companies used GenAI in 2024; NY Fed survey: firms plan to retrain workforces, widespread layoffs limited, but AI has led firms to scale back hiring; ~$3 trillion of new data-center capacity projected; financial-sector AI adoption concentrated in operational efficiency, with core functions (credit, fraud, trading) facing challenges—decisions must be controlled, legally precise, explainable, replicable; risks include bias in consumer lending and AI trading causing tacit collusion/manipulation/systemic risk; Fed has an AI program and governance framework, 'hands on keys' approach, using GenAI for legacy-code translation, unit tests, cloud migration [D48][D49][D50][D51].

Jefferson (2025-11-21, Cleveland): ~55% of working-age adults used generative AI (St. Louis Fed, Aug 2025); AI boosts productivity but may cause job loss, especially for younger/less-experienced workers; net employment effect 'highly uncertain'; AI could create economic slack; on prices, productivity could lower costs but data centers compete for land/energy; 'too soon to tell' for monetary policy—counsels humility; 30% of market contacts cited a turn in AI sentiment as a salient financial-stability risk (up from 9% in spring); argues current AI market differs from dot-com: AI firms have established earnings, lower P/E ratios, only ~50 publicly traded AI-focused firms vs 1,000+ dot-coms; but flags rising AI debt issuance as a watch item [D53][D54][D55][D56].

Cook (2025-07-17, NBER): AI is at an 'inflection point' and the next general-purpose technology; four principles for responsible AI adoption: strong governance/risk management with humans in the loop, staff education/training, empowerment (learn by doing), and experimentation; FOMC is not using AI in developing or setting policy, only for staff tasks (writing, coding, research); cites Fed research (LLMs understanding FOMC minutes, synthetic forecasters, ML for crisis forecasting, real-time layoff tracking); cautions LLMs suffer look-ahead bias and unreliable historical recall; AI likely to boost productivity and reduce inflationary pressures over time but could boost prices in the interim via investment surge [D70][D71][D72][D73][D74].

Taking "the Federal Reserve" to mean the official views and statements of Fed officials (Governors, Vice Chairs, the Chair) and Fed research staff as found in the local collection of speeches and notes from 2025–2026: the Fed describes AI as a transformative general-purpose technology that will raise productivity and growth, is actively deploying AI in its own operations (while the FOMC does not use AI to set policy), and is monitoring AI's financial-stability risks—algorithmic trading, cyber, and leveraged AI-infrastructure investment. The most recent and authoritative statements (Governor Lisa D. Cook, September 28, 2026) frame AI investment as a current, net inflationary pressure that will delay disinflation, while earlier 2025 statements (Governors Barr, Jefferson) emphasized AI's ultimately disinflationary productivity gains and counseled humility on the near-term monetary-policy effect.

## Consensus across Fed officials
- **AI as a general-purpose technology.** Governor Cook calls AI "the most significant technological shift of our lifetime," on par with the steam engine, electricity, and the internet, affecting monetary policy, financial stability, supervision, and Fed operations [D1]. Governor Waller (February 24, 2026) calls it a technological revolution unlike any in his lifetime, and the Fed is "no different" in trying to incorporate it [D28].
- **The Fed uses AI internally; the FOMC does not use AI to set policy.** Cook states clearly that "the Federal Open Market Committee is not using AI in developing or setting policy," but the Fed uses AI for financial-stability analysis and staff tasks (writing, coding, research) [D37][D70]. Waller details a "System-first" approach with a common internal general-purpose AI platform for all Reserve Bank employees, coding assistants for developers, and AI embedded in enterprise workflows; AI use is not optional and baseline literacy is built into performance goals [D28][D29][D31].
- **Financial-stability risks to monitor.** Officials consistently flag AI-driven algorithmic trading (correlated trading, model collusion, manipulation, concentration), cyber risk from LLMs/agentic AI, and rising debt/leverage to finance AI infrastructure [D36][D37][D10].

## Distinct perspectives
- **Near-term inflation effect.** Cook (May 27, 2026, and September 28, 2026) argues AI investment is now a net inflationary pressure—chips, computers, software prices surging; electricity and water up ~5% over the past year; core goods running >3% annual pace—and expects only "modest disinflation within the next few years" from productivity, not in time to offset broadening pressure [D2][D34][D6]. By contrast, Barr (November 11, 2025) and Jefferson (November 21, 2025) frame AI's productivity gains as ultimately disinflationary, with Jefferson saying it is "too soon to tell" for monetary policy and counseling humility [D33][D35].
- **Labor market.** Cook and Barr stress that AI-related job losses could precede job gains and hit young/entry-level workers; Cook is "highly attentive" to a supply-side skills-mismatch scenario where the Fed would have limited tools [D4][D34]. Jefferson is more balanced, calling the net employment effect "highly uncertain" [D53]. Fed research (Liu & Webber, March 2026) finds no evidence of a reduction in job postings for firms/industries with higher AI adoption, though skill requirements and wage premia are shifting [D39].
- **Supervision.** Vice Chair Bowman is the most pro-innovation, urging proportionality and a lighter touch for smaller banks, and noting the Fed/OCC/FDIC amended model-risk guidance to exclude generative/agentic AI [D7][D8][D10].
- **Dot-com comparison.** Jefferson argues the current AI market differs from the late-1990s bubble (established earnings, lower P/E, ~50 publicly traded AI-focused firms vs. 1,000+ dot-coms), though he flags rising AI debt as a watch item [D56].

question: How healthy is the US banking system according to the Fed?
answer:
According to the Federal Reserve's most recent official assessments, the U.S. banking system is **strong, sound, and resilient**, with capital and liquidity levels well above regulatory requirements and profitability at or above historical averages. The June 2026 Supervision and Regulation Report explicitly states that "The U.S. banking system continues to maintain strong capital and liquidity levels while maintaining strong profitability and healthy loan growth" and that banks are "well positioned to continue to support a growing economy" [D9]. The 2026 stress test results confirm that the 32 largest banks have sufficient capital to absorb nearly $708 billion in losses under a severe recession scenario while continuing to lend [D35]. However, the Fed identifies specific vulnerabilities in commercial real estate (CRE), private credit, and agriculture, and there is a notable internal divergence between Fed officials regarding the direction of supervisory reforms.

### Capital, Liquidity, and Profitability
The Fed’s June 2026 Supervision and Regulation Report highlights robust fundamental metrics:
*   **Capital:** Over 99% of all banks were well capitalized as of Q4 2025. Aggregate Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratios were approximately 13% for both large and small banks, roughly unchanged from the prior year. Aggregate tangible common equity reached a record $2.23 trillion, aided by unrealized losses on available-for-sale securities falling to $98 billion (less than one-third of 2022 peaks) [D11].
*   **Liquidity:** Liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) banks held liquidity well above requirements. Aggregate deposits hit a historical high of $19.5 trillion by February 2026. While uninsured deposits rose slightly from 2023–24 lows, they remained below 2022 levels; conversely, reliance on wholesale funding fell slightly in the second half of 2025, though it remained above 2022 levels [D11][D12].
*   **Profitability:** Return on average assets (ROAA) was ~1.1% and return on equity (ROE) was ~11.2% at the end of 2025. In Q1 2026, large-bank ROE jumped to 14% (from 12% in Q4 2025) driven by record capital markets revenues, though net interest income was flat quarter-over-quarter [D28][D30].
*   **Market Confidence:** Credit default swap (CDS) spreads for the largest banks ended 2025 near their lowest levels since 2015 (though they rose in March–April 2026), and the market leverage ratio sits near a 10-year high, indicating strong market confidence in bank financial strength [D29].

### 2026 Stress Test Results
The 2026 stress test results demonstrate that the 32 largest banks can withstand a severe global recession:
*   **Resilience:** Banks have sufficient capital to absorb nearly $708 billion in losses. The aggregate CET1 ratio falls from an actual 12.8% (Q4 2025) to a projected minimum of 11.2% (Q4 2027), then recovers to 12.7% by Q1 2028. This 1.6 percentage point decline is smaller than in recent years [D35][D36].
*   **Compliance:** All 32 banks’ post-stress CET1 ratios remain above the 4.5% regulatory minimum throughout the projection horizon. Individual bank minimum CET1 ratios range from 6.7% (First Citizens) to 32.2% (Charles Schwab) [D35][D58].
*   **Scenario Assumptions:** The "severely adverse" scenario assumes a severe global recession with real GDP falling 4.6% peak-to-trough, equity prices dropping ~58%, house prices falling 30%, commercial real estate prices falling 39%, and unemployment rising 5.5 percentage points to 10% [D14][D37].
*   **Loss Drivers:** Credit cards represent the largest loss category (29% of total losses, with a 17.1% loss rate), followed by commercial and industrial loans (22%) and CRE (11%) [D82][D83].

### Identified Vulnerabilities and Risks
Despite overall strength, the Fed highlights specific areas of concern:
*   **Commercial Real Estate (CRE):** Delinquencies on CRE and consumer loans remain above 10-year averages, partly because office space demand has not returned to pre-pandemic levels. Supervisors are closely monitoring community and regional banks concentrated in CRE (especially office and multifamily) due to elevated interest rates and lower property values affecting borrowers' ability to refinance [D48][D90]. In Q2 2025, the CRE delinquency rate was ~1.5% (roughly double the 10-year average), and office loan delinquencies at large banks remained near 10% [D89].
*   **Private Credit/NDFI:** Several high-profile non-depository financial institution (NDFI) defaults have raised concerns about the private credit sector. Some banks are revisiting collateral management practices for these exposures [D28].
*   **Agriculture:** Community banks face tight profit margins in agriculture-related businesses, with lending volumes and loan sizes increasing [D91].
*   **Large Bank Capital Trends:** Aggregate CET1 for large banks declined to 12% in Q1 2026 as shareholder distributions and risk-weighted asset growth outpaced earnings, though all remained well capitalized [D31].

### Supervisory Commentary and Internal Divergence
While Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman and Governor Michael S. Barr agree that the banking system is currently "sound and resilient," they sharply diverge on the direction of supervisory reforms:
*   **Vice Chair Bowman (Testimony, Dec 2025 & Feb 2026):** Emphasizes the system's strength and frames recent regulatory changes (LFI ratings reform, CAMELS review, stress test transparency) as necessary modernization to restore transparency and risk-based focus. She highlights competitive pressure from nonbanks and regulatory burden on community banks as key issues [D22][D25].
*   **Governor Barr (Speech, Nov 2025):** Argues the system is at a "moment of inflection" where growing pressures to weaken supervision—such as a planned 30% cut to the Board's Supervision and Regulation division by end-2026, diluted ratings, and redefined "unsafe and unsound" standards—threaten to recreate pre-crisis vulnerabilities. He warns that these changes will "tie examiners' hands" and erode the ability to detect risks early, stating that "the bill always comes due" for weakened supervision [D19][D21][D42][D43].

In summary, the Fed’s data and stress tests confirm a highly resilient banking system with strong capital and profitability, but supervisors remain vigilant regarding CRE and private credit risks, while internal debates continue over the adequacy of the supervisory framework to detect future vulnerabilities.

The aggregate CET1 ratio falls from an actual 12.8% (2025:Q4) to a projected minimum of 11.2% (in the fourth projection quarter, 2027:Q4), then recovers to 12.7% by 2028:Q1 — a 1.6 percentage point aggregate decline, smaller than in recent years [D35][D36][D87]. All 32 banks' post-stress CET1 ratios remain above the 4.5% regulatory minimum throughout the horizon; individual bank minimum CET1 ratios range from 6.7% (First Citizens) to 32.2% (Charles Schwab), with a median decline of 1.8 percentage points [D35][D58][D60]. The scenario assumes a severe global recession: real GDP falls 4.6% peak-to-trough, equity prices fall ~58%, house prices fall 30%, commercial real estate prices fall 39%, and unemployment rises 5.5 p.p. from 4.5% to a peak of 10% [D37][D14]. Notable findings: credit cards are the largest loss category (29% of total losses, 17.1% aggregate loss rate); commercial loan losses (48%) exceed consumer (41%); Synchrony Financial has the highest total loan loss rate (20.7%); and the smaller aggregate capital decline vs. 2025 reflects higher projected net interest income partly offsetting greater loan losses and smaller unrealized AFS gains [D36][D82][D83][D84].

data.answer: The three documents show a sharp divergence between Governor Barr and Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman on the direction of banking supervision, though both agree the banking system is currently sound. Barr (speech, 2025-11-18) argues the system is at a "moment of inflection" where growing pressures to weaken supervision—reduced examiner coverage, diluted ratings, redefined "unsafe and unsound" standards—threaten to recreate pre-crisis vulnerabilities. He does not cite specific sector risks (e.g., CRE) but warns that weakened forward-looking tools (stress tests, horizontal reviews) and a 30% planned cut to the Board's Supervision and Regulation division by end-2026 will erode the ability to detect risks early. Bowman (testimony, 2025-12-02 and 2026-02-26) emphasizes the system's current strength—strong capital, liquidity, profitability, declining non-performing loans—and frames the same regulatory changes (LFI ratings reform, CAMELS review, MRA recalibration, stress test transparency) as necessary modernization and tailoring, not weakening. Her key risk emphasis is competitive pressure from nonbanks and regulatory burden on community banks, not supervisory capacity. The core disagreement: Barr views the 2025-2026 reforms as dangerous deregulation that will "tie examiners' hands"; Bowman views them as restoring transparency, objectivity, and risk-based focus.
key_facts: Barr: 'We are now, I believe, at a moment of inflection in the regulatory and supervisory approaches that help keep banks healthy. There are growing pressures to weaken supervision—to scale back examiner coverage, to dilute ratings systems, and to redefine "unsafe and unsound"—in ways that will make it harder for examiners to act before it is too late.' [D19]

Barr: The Board's final rule on the LFI rating system 'makes changes… Poor performance is being deemphasized, which is tantamount to grade inflation… These changes reduce incentives for large banks to fix serious management problems.' He also criticized the FDIC/OCC proposed rule limiting enforcement actions for 'unsafe or unsound practices' as 'effectively tying examiners' hands.' [D21]

Barr: 'Recently announced plans to reduce staffing in the Board's Supervision and Regulation division by 30 percent by the end of 2026 will impair supervisors' ability to act with the speed, force, and agility appropriate to the risks facing individual banks and the financial system.' [D42]

Barr: The October 2025 stress test proposal 'risk[s] turning the stress test into a rigid exercise that offers false confidence by producing overly optimistic results driven by less conservative modeling and opportunities for banks to game the process.' [D41]
Barr: 'The vulnerabilities that weaker supervision and regulation create may not be visible in the short term. They rarely are. But experience tells us that the bill always comes due.' [D43]

Bowman (2025-12-02): 'The banking system remains sound and resilient. Banks continue to report strong capital ratios and significant liquidity buffers… The overall health of the banking sector is demonstrated by continued growth in lending, a decline in non-performing loans across most categories, and strong profitability.' [D22]

Bowman (2026-02-26): Same assessment: 'The banking system remains sound and resilient… continued growth in lending, a decline in non-performing loans across most categories, and strong profitability.' She adds: 'non-bank financial institutions continue to increase their share of the total lending market, creating strong competition for regulated banks without facing the same capital, liquidity, and other prudential standards.' [D25]

Bowman (2025-12-02): On the LFI ratings reform she supports: 'Prior to the recent modification of the Large Financial Institution (LFI) ratings system, banks have often been labeled as not "well managed" despite strong capital and liquidity positions. To address this shortcoming, the Board recently finalized revisions to the LFI ratings system that address the mismatch between ratings and overall firm condition.' [D44]

Bowman (2026-02-26): 'An effective supervisory framework must focus on the core material risks to banks operations and to the stability of the broader financial system. Let me be clear: those core material risks include non-financial risks where they pose threats to safety and soundness.' She also announced an 'independent third-party review of the 2023 bank failures' and publication of internal supervisory manuals. [D27][D45]

Bowman (both testimonies): On stress testing, describes the October 2025 proposal positively: 'The proposed model changes reduce volatility in capital requirements by addressing some shortcomings in our models and by providing full transparency.' [D26]

Bowman (both testimonies): 'The Board officially ended the practice of using reputational risk in our supervisory program' and proposed a regulation to prevent supervisors from compelling banks to debank customers based on constitutionally protected beliefs. [D44][D45]

data.answer: The June 2026 Supervision and Regulation Report assesses the U.S. banking system as strong and well positioned to support a growing economy. The Introduction's headline conclusion is: "The U.S. banking system continues to maintain strong capital and liquidity levels while maintaining strong profitability and healthy loan growth. U.S. banks are well positioned to continue to support a growing economy" [D9]. Capital levels remain strong: over 99% of banks were well capitalized as of Q4 2025, with aggregate CET1 ratios of about 13% for both large and small banks (roughly unchanged year-over-year), and aggregate tangible common equity at a record $2.23 trillion, aided by AFS unrealized losses falling to $98 billion (less than one-third of 2022 peaks) [D11]. Liquidity and funding conditions "shifted slightly but remain solid": LCR banks held liquidity well above requirements, deposits hit a record $19.5 trillion by February 2026, uninsured deposits rose slightly from 2023–24 lows but stayed below 2022 levels, and wholesale funding reliance fell slightly in H2 2025 but remained above 2022 levels [D11][D12]. Asset quality: loan growth was strong (loans up 5.6% in 2025, with C&I accelerating in H2 2025), but delinquency rates rose slightly across consumer, CRE, C&I, and RRE categories, lifting the total delinquency rate to 1.6% — still well below the ~3% long-run historical average [D13][D28]. Profitability was healthy: ROAA of ~1.1% and ROE of ~11.2% at end-2025, with net interest margins rising slightly on lower funding costs [D28]; in Q1 2026, large-bank ROE jumped to 14% (from 12% in Q4 2025) on record capital markets revenues, while net interest income was flat quarter-over-quarter [D30]. Market indicators showed confidence: CDS spreads for the largest banks ended 2025 near their lowest since 2015 (though they rose in March–April 2026), and the market leverage ratio sits near a 10-year high [D29]. Identified vulnerabilities/risks: (1) NDFI/private credit — high-profile NDFI defaults have raised concern about the private credit sector, and some banks are revisiting collateral management practices for these exposures [D28]; (2) CRE — supervisors continue to monitor CBOs/RBOs concentrated in CRE (especially office and multifamily), noting elevated rates and lower property values may affect borrowers' ability to refinance, and CRE and consumer delinquencies remain above 10-year averages partly because office-space demand has not returned to pre-pandemic levels [D90]; (3) agriculture concentrations at community banks, with tight profit margins [D91]; (4) at large banks, Q1 2026 CET1 ratios declined quarter-over-quarter (aggregate 12% at end-Q1 2026) as distributions and RWA growth outpaced earnings, though all remained well capitalized [D31]. Supervisory ratings: most large financial institutions were rated satisfactory/"well-managed" across all LFI components as of 1/31/2026, with weaknesses identified in financial risk management (capital planning, liquidity), operational resilience, and BSA/AML compliance; outstanding MR(I)As at large institutions decreased in H2 2025 [D92].

data.answer:
According to the Federal Reserve's most recent official assessments, the U.S. banking system is **strong, sound, and resilient**, with capital and liquidity levels well above regulatory requirements and profitability at or above historical averages. The June 2026 Supervision and Regulation Report explicitly states that "The U.S. banking system continues to maintain strong capital and liquidity levels while maintaining strong profitability and healthy loan growth" and that banks are "well positioned to continue to support a growing economy" [D9]. The 2026 stress test results confirm that the 32 largest banks have sufficient capital to absorb nearly $708 billion in losses under a severe recession scenario while continuing to lend [D35]. However, the Fed identifies specific vulnerabilities in commercial real estate (CRE), private credit, and agriculture, and there is a notable internal divergence between Fed officials regarding the direction of supervisory reforms.

### Capital, Liquidity, and Profitability
The Fed’s June 2026 Supervision and Regulation Report highlights robust fundamental metrics:
*   **Capital:** Over 99% of all banks were well capitalized as of Q4 2025. Aggregate Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratios were approximately 13% for both large and small banks, roughly unchanged from the prior year. Aggregate tangible common equity reached a record $2.23 trillion, aided by unrealized losses on available-for-sale securities falling to $98 billion (less than one-third of 2022 peaks) [D11].
*   **Liquidity:** Liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) banks held liquidity well above requirements. Aggregate deposits hit a historical high of $19.5 trillion by February 2026. While uninsured deposits and wholesale funding reliance rose slightly from 2023–24 lows, they remained below 2022 levels [D11][D12].
*   **Profitability:** Return on average assets (ROAA) was ~1.1% and return on equity (ROE) was ~11.2% at the end of 2025. In Q1 2026, large-bank ROE jumped to 14% (from 12% in Q4 2025) driven by record capital markets revenues, though net interest income was flat quarter-over-quarter [D28][D30].
*   **Market Confidence:** Credit default swap (CDS) spreads for the largest banks ended 2025 near their lowest levels since 2015, and the market leverage ratio sits near a 10-year high, indicating strong market confidence in bank financial strength [D29].

### 2026 Stress Test Results
Published on June 24, 2026, the stress test results demonstrate that the 32 largest banks can withstand a severe global recession:
*   **Resilience:** Banks have sufficient capital to absorb nearly $708 billion in losses. The aggregate CET1 ratio falls from an actual 12.8% (Q4 2025) to a projected minimum of 11.2% (Q4 2027), then recovers to 12.7% by Q1 2028. This 1.6 percentage point decline is smaller than in recent years [D35][D36].
*   **Compliance:** All 32 banks’ post-stress CET1 ratios remain above the 4.5% regulatory minimum throughout the projection horizon. Individual bank minimum CET1 ratios range from 6.7% (First Citizens) to 32.2% (Charles Schwab) [D35][D58].
*   **Scenario Assumptions:** The "severely adverse" scenario assumes a severe global recession with real GDP falling 4.6% peak-to-trough, equity prices dropping ~58%, house prices falling 30%, commercial real estate prices falling 39%, and unemployment rising 5.5 percentage points to 10% [D14][D37].
*   **Loss Drivers:** Credit cards represent the largest loss category (29% of total losses, with a 17.1% loss rate), followed by commercial and industrial loans (22%) and CRE (11%) [D82][D83].

### Identified Vulnerabilities and Risks
Despite overall strength, the Fed highlights specific areas of concern:
*   **Commercial Real Estate (CRE):** Delinquencies on CRE and consumer loans remain above 10-year averages, partly because office space demand has not returned to pre-pandemic levels. Supervisors are closely monitoring community and regional banks concentrated in CRE (especially office and multifamily) due to elevated interest rates and lower property values affecting borrowers' ability to refinance [D48][D90]. In Q2 2025, the CRE delinquency rate was ~1.5% (roughly double the 10-year average), and office loan delinquencies at large banks remained near 10% [D89].
*   **Private Credit/NDFI:** Several high-profile non-depository financial institution (NDFI) defaults have raised concerns about the private credit sector. Some banks are revisiting collateral management practices for these exposures [D28].
*   **Agriculture:** Community banks face tight profit margins in agriculture-related businesses, with lending volumes and loan sizes increasing [D91].
*   **Large Bank Capital Trends:** Aggregate CET1 for large banks declined to 12% in Q1 2026 as shareholder distributions and risk-weighted asset growth outpaced earnings, though all remained well capitalized [D31].

### Supervisory Commentary and Internal Divergence
While Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman and Governor Michael S. Barr agree that the banking system is currently "sound and resilient," they sharply diverge on the direction of supervisory reforms:
*   **Vice Chair Bowman (Testimony, Dec 2025 & Feb 2026):** Emphasizes the system's strength and frames recent regulatory changes (LFI ratings reform, CAMELS review, stress test transparency) as necessary modernization to restore transparency and risk-based focus. She highlights competitive pressure from nonbanks and regulatory burden on community banks as key issues [D22][D25].
*   **Governor Barr (Speech, Nov 2025):** Argues the system is at a "moment of inflection" where growing pressures to weaken supervision—such as a planned 30% cut to the Board's Supervision and Regulation division by end-2026, diluted ratings, and redefined "unsafe and unsound" standards—threaten to recreate pre-crisis vulnerabilities. He warns that these changes will "tie examiners' hands" and erode the ability to detect risks early, stating that "the bill always comes due" for weakened supervision [D19][D21][D42][D43].

In summary, the Fed’s data and stress tests confirm a highly resilient banking system with strong capital and profitability, but supervisors remain vigilant regarding CRE and private credit risks, while internal debates continue over the adequacy of the supervisory framework to detect future vulnerabilities.

*   **Compliance:** All 32 banks’ post-stress CET1 ratios remain above the 4.5% regulatory minimum throughout the projection horizon. Individual bank minimum CET1 ratios range from 6.7% (First Citizens) to 32.2% (Charles Schwab) [D35][D58].
*   **Scenario Assumptions:** The "severely adverse" scenario assumes a severe global recession with real GDP falling 4.6% peak-to-trough, equity prices dropping ~58%, house prices falling 30%, commercial real estate prices falling 39%, and unemployment rising 5.5 percentage points to 10% [D14][D37].
*   **Loss Drivers:** Credit cards represent the largest loss category (29% of total losses, with a 17.1% loss rate), followed by commercial and industrial loans (22%) and CRE (11%) [D82][D83].

### Identified Vulnerabilities and Risks
Despite overall strength, the Fed highlights specific areas of concern:
*   **Commercial Real Estate (CRE):** Delinquencies on CRE and consumer loans remain above 10-year averages, partly because office space demand has not returned to pre-pandemic levels. Supervisors are closely monitoring community and regional banks concentrated in CRE (especially office and multifamily) due to elevated interest rates and lower property values affecting borrowers' ability to refinance [D48][D90]. In Q2 2025, the CRE delinquency rate was ~1.5% (roughly double the 10-year average), and office loan delinquencies at large banks remained near 10% [D89].
*   **Private Credit/NDFI:** Several high-profile non-depository financial institution (NDFI) defaults have raised concerns about the private credit sector. Some banks are revisiting collateral management practices for these exposures [D28].
*   **Agriculture:** Community banks face tight profit margins in agriculture-related businesses, with lending volumes and loan sizes increasing [D91].
*   **Large Bank Capital Trends:** Aggregate CET1 for large banks declined to 12% in Q1 2026 as shareholder distributions and risk-weighted asset growth outpaced earnings, though all remained well capitalized [D31].

### Supervisory Commentary and Internal Divergence
While Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman and Governor Michael S. Barr agree that the banking system is currently "sound and resilient," they sharply diverge on the direction of supervisory reforms:
*   **Vice Chair Bowman (Testimony, Dec 2025 & Feb 2026):** Emphasizes the system's strength and frames recent regulatory changes (LFI ratings reform, CAMELS review, stress test transparency) as necessary modernization to restore transparency and risk-based focus. She highlights competitive pressure from nonbanks and regulatory burden on community banks as key issues [D22][D25].
*   **Governor Barr (Speech, Nov 2025):** Argues the system is at a "moment of inflection" where growing pressures to weaken supervision—such as a planned 30% cut to the Board's Supervision and Regulation division by end-2026, diluted ratings, and redefined "unsafe and unsound" standards—threaten to recreate pre-crisis vulnerabilities. He warns that these changes will "tie examiners' hands" and erode the ability to detect risks early, stating that "the bill always comes due" for weakened supervision [D19][D21][D42][D43].

In summary, the Fed’s data and stress tests confirm a highly resilient banking system with strong capital and profitability, but supervisors remain vigilant regarding CRE and private credit risks, while internal debates continue over the adequacy of the supervisory framework to detect future vulnerabilities.

judge: The answer correctly states the main point that the Fed views the U.S. banking system as healthy/strong/sound/resilient, and it covers the June 2026 Supervision and Regulation Report points (strong capital, liquidity, profitability, healthy loan growth, most banks well capitalized through year-end 2025) and the 2026 stress test facts (all banks above minimums, aggregate CET1 decline of 1.6 points to an 11.2% minimum). It also names pockets of risk. However, it does not explicitly cite the May 2026 Financial Stability Report and omits or only partially captures some of its key facts, such as historically high regulatory capital ratios, fair-value losses on fixed-rate assets being improved but still elevated, and most banks holding high liquid assets. Therefore it is partially correct rather than fully correct.

question: What is the Fed doing about stablecoins?
answer:
The Federal Reserve is actively implementing the GENIUS Act (Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act) by proposing a comprehensive regulatory framework for payment stablecoins, rescinding older restrictive supervisory guidance, and conducting extensive research on the monetary and financial stability implications of stablecoin adoption. The Board’s most recent action, on September 24, 2026, was to request public comment on two proposals that would establish the core prudential and application requirements for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers [D56].

### Regulatory and Supervisory Actions

The Fed’s regulatory approach has shifted from cautious supervision to active rulemaking under the GENIUS Act, which was signed into law in July 2025 [D66][D87]. Key actions include:

*   **Proposed Regulatory Framework (September 24, 2026):** The Board requested public comment on two proposals to establish a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers [D56].
    *   **Proposal 1:** Requires full backing of stablecoins with permissible reserve assets (e.g., short-term Treasury bills, high-quality liquid assets), establishes standardized capital requirements for credit and operational risks, sets risk management standards, introduces safekeeping rules, and clarifies the permissibility of stablecoin activities for Board-supervised banks [D56].
    *   **Proposal 2:** Establishes a tailored application process for Board-supervised banks seeking to issue payment stablecoins, including requirements for business plans and financial information, as well as a process for appeals, hearings, and final determinations [D56].
*   **Customer Identification Program (June 18, 2026):** The Board, jointly with four other agencies, requested comment on a proposal requiring certain payment stablecoin issuers to maintain an effective customer identification program comparable to bank and credit union requirements [D60].
*   **Rescission of Older Guidance (April 24, 2025):** The Board withdrew its 2022 supervisory letter requiring advance notification of bank crypto-asset activities and its 2023 supervisory nonobjection process for dollar token activities, stating these actions ensure expectations remain aligned with evolving risks and support innovation [D78].
*   **Supervisory Priorities:** Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman testified in February 2026 that the Fed is working with other banking regulators to develop capital and liquidity regulations for stablecoin issuers as required by the GENIUS Act and is providing clarity on the treatment of digital assets to encourage responsible innovation [D57].

### Research on Monetary Policy and Financial Stability

Fed officials and staff have published extensive research analyzing how stablecoins could affect the economy, with a focus on monetary policy, bank deposits, and financial stability.

**Monetary Policy and Money Supply**
*   **Neutral Interest Rate (r*):** Governor Stephen Miran (November 2025) argued that stablecoins could become a "multitrillion dollar elephant in the room," with Fed staff estimates projecting $1–3 trillion in stablecoin uptake by the end of the decade [D75][D76]. This growth would boost demand for U.S. Treasury bills and other dollar liquid assets, potentially lowering the neutral interest rate (r*) by up to 40 basis points [D75][D77].
*   **Monetary Aggregates:** A September 2026 FEDS Note by Payne and Styczynski found that payment stablecoins are not currently included in U.S. monetary aggregates [D69]. Depending on their primary use, they could be classified as M1 (if used as a medium of exchange) or non-M1 M2 (if used as a store of value), though measurement challenges exist regarding double-counting of reserve assets and geographic scope [D69][D85][D86].

**Banking System and Deposits**
*   **Deposit Disintermediation:** Research indicates the impact on bank deposits depends critically on how stablecoin issuers manage reserves [D88]. If issuers hold reserves as bank deposits, aggregate deposits may remain largely unchanged but shift toward concentrated, uninsured wholesale deposits [D88][D89]. If reserves are held in Treasury bills or if issuers gain access to Federal Reserve master accounts paying interest, bank deposits could fall substantially, leading to greater disintermediation [D89][D90].
*   **Bank Adaptation:** A May 2026 FEDS Note by Hempel, Perez-Sangimino, and Wang noted that historically, banks have adapted to disintermediation threats (e.g., from money market funds and PayPal) through regulatory advocacy, product innovation, and strategic participation in the new ecosystem [D72][D24].

**Financial Stability**
*   **Run Risk and Reserve Quality:** Governor Michael Barr (March 2026) emphasized that stablecoins are "stable only if they can be reliably and promptly redeemed at par in a wide range of conditions," highlighting the critical importance of reserve asset quality and liquidity [D91]. He noted that the GENIUS Act’s requirement for 1:1 backing in safe, liquid assets is the primary mitigation tool, but implementation details regarding capital, liquidity, and anti-money laundering controls remain key concerns [D91][D92].
*   **Structural Vulnerabilities:** An April 2026 FEDS Note by Carapella, Lubis, and Vardoulakis identified three structural vulnerabilities: complex intermediation chains creating contagion risk, vertical integration complicating risk assessment, and accelerating retail adoption [D96][D97][D98]. The stablecoin market capitalization reached $317 billion as of April 6, 2026, representing more than 50% growth since early 2025 [D97].

### Historical Context

The Fed’s approach has evolved significantly since 2022:
*   **2022:** The Board issued SR 22-6/CA 22-6, requiring supervised banks to determine the legality of crypto-asset activities and notify the Fed before engaging in them [D51][D64].
*   **2023:** The Fed launched the Novel Activities Supervision Program with dedicated staff for crypto-assets and distributed ledger technology [D53][D61]. It also issued interagency statements on crypto risks, including runs on stablecoins, and established a supervisory nonobjection process for dollar token activities [D1][D61][D62].
*   **2024:** The focus shifted toward research and monitoring, with staff studying stablecoins, tokenization, and AI in payments, while engaging with international bodies like the BIS and FSB [D3].

This evolution reflects a transition from initial caution and notification requirements to a more structured, rule-based framework designed to integrate stablecoins into the financial system while managing associated risks.

data.answer: Recent Fed officials' speeches and FEDS Notes present a nuanced, largely conditional view of stablecoins' implications. On monetary policy, Governor Miran (Nov 2025) argues stablecoins could become a "multitrillion dollar elephant in the room," with Fed staff estimates projecting $1–3 trillion of stablecoin growth by the end of the decade; this would boost demand for T-bills and other dollar liquid assets, potentially lowering the neutral rate (r*) by up to ~40 bps (citing Azzimonti & Quadrini 2024), and could disintermediate banks if deposits flow into stablecoins. On the money supply, the Sept 2026 FEDS Note (Payne & Styczynski) finds payment stablecoins are not currently in the monetary aggregates but could be placed in M1 (if used as a medium of exchange) or non-M1 M2 (if used as a store of value), with measurement challenges around double-counting and geographic scope. On cross-border payments, the March 2026 FEDS Note (Kim, Ruprecht & Styczynski) shows stablecoins could reduce frictions by shortening payment chains and reducing reliance on correspondent banks, but would affect the market for domestic/foreign liquid assets and the central bank's balance sheet and reserve management. On bank deposits, the Dec 2025 FEDS Note (Wang) and May 2026 FEDS Note (Hempel et al.) find the effect depends critically on reserve composition: if issuers hold reserves as bank deposits, aggregate deposits are largely maintained but composition shifts toward concentrated, uninsured wholesale deposits; if reserves go to T-bills or Fed master accounts, deposits could fall substantially. On financial stability, Governor Barr (Mar 2026) and the April 2026 FEDS Note (Carapella et al.) emphasize run risk, reserve asset quality/liquidity, complex intermediation chains, vertical integration, and opacity as key vulnerabilities, with the GENIUS Act's 1:1 reserve backing as the primary mitigation.
key_facts: Miran (Nov 7, 2025): stablecoins may become a 'multitrillion dollar elephant in the room for central bankers'; Fed staff inter-quartile range projects $1–3 trillion stablecoin uptake by end of decade; could put up to 40 bps downward pressure on interest rates (citing Azzimonti & Quadrini 2024); GENIUS Act requires 1:1 backing in safe, liquid USD assets [D75][D76][D77]

Payne & Styczynski FEDS Note (Sept 4, 2026): payment stablecoins not currently in monetary aggregates; could be M1 (medium of exchange) or non-M1 M2 (store of value) depending on use case; measurement challenges include double-counting risk (backing assets like bank deposits already in aggregates) and geographic scope (global circulation on public blockchains) [D69][D85][D86][D87]

Kim, Ruprecht & Styczynski FEDS Note (Mar 30, 2026): stablecoins could reduce cross-border payment frictions by shortening payment chains and reducing correspondent bank reliance; three reserve scenarios (bank deposits, T-bills, Fed reserves) each have different implications for central bank balance sheet and reserve management; demand for USD reserves might decrease while demand for T-bills might increase [D66][D67][D68][D93][D94]

Wang FEDS Note (Dec 17, 2025): if stablecoin issuers hold reserves primarily as bank deposits, aggregate banking system deposits remain largely unchanged but composition shifts to concentrated uninsured wholesale deposits; if reserves go to T-bills/repos/MMFs, deposits could reduce; if issuers gain Fed master account access paying IORB, maximum bank disintermediation occurs [D88][D89][D90]

Hempel, Perez-Sangimino & Wang FEDS Note (May 1, 2026): historical evidence (MMFs, PayPal) shows banks adapt to disintermediation threats through regulatory advocacy, product innovation, and strategic participation; stablecoins integrate balance-holding and payment functionality, competing for both transaction balances and payment flows; whether stablecoins become a major source of disintermediation depends on scale, reserve structure, and regulatory design [D72][D24]

Barr speech (Mar 31, 2026): financial stability concern is that stablecoins are 'stable only if they can be reliably and promptly redeemed at par in a wide range of conditions'; GENIUS Act's primary tool is limiting permissible reserve assets to high-quality, highly liquid assets; key implementation issues include reserve asset regulation, regulatory arbitrage, capital/liquidity requirements, AML controls, and consumer protection [D91][D92]

Carapella, Lubis & Vardoulakis FEDS Note (Apr 8, 2026): stablecoin market cap reached $317 billion as of April 6, 2026 (50%+ growth since early 2025); three structural vulnerabilities: (1) complex intermediation chains creating contagion risk and opacity, (2) vertical integration complicating risk assessment, (3) accelerating retail adoption through digital wallet partnerships; run risk can propagate through interconnections within digital asset ecosystem and across traditional financial system [D96][D97][D98]

Waller speech (Feb 12, 2025): stablecoins involved in over 80% of trading volume on major centralized crypto exchanges; ~99% of stablecoin market cap is USD-denominated; three use cases: crypto trading, dollar access/store of value, and cross-border payments ('stablecoin sandwich' model); stablecoins have potential to maintain and extend the dollar's international role [D30][D37]

Barr speech (Oct 16, 2025): stablecoins can reduce remittance costs, especially to jurisdictions with less-developed payment systems; stablecoin acceptance networks have arisen in some corridors to reduce on/off-ramp fees; for stablecoins to reach their potential, additional guardrails are needed to protect households, businesses, and the financial system [D31][D36]

data.answer: The three Board Annual Reports document a clear evolution in the Fed's crypto-asset and stablecoin approach. In 2022, the Fed issued SR 22-6/CA 22-6, "Engagement in Crypto-Asset-Related Activities by Federal Reserve-Supervised Banking Organizations," establishing expectations that supervised banks determine the legality of crypto-asset activities and notify the Fed before engaging in them, while noting crypto-assets pose IT/operations, AML, consumer protection, and financial stability risks [D51][D64]. In 2023, the Fed System launched the Novel Activities Supervision Program (SR 23-7, Aug. 8, 2023) with dedicated staff to supervise crypto-asset, distributed-ledger, and technology-driven nonbank partnership activities [D53][D61][D82]; issued interagency statements on key crypto risks (Jan. 3, 2023, including runs on stablecoins, volatility, and legal uncertainty) and on crypto liquidity risk (Feb. 23, 2023) [D1][D61][D62]; and published SR 23-08/CA 23-08 (Aug. 8, 2023) describing the supervisory nonobjection process for state member banks engaging in certain "dollar token" activities, building on the Board's Jan. 27, 2023 Policy Statement on section 9(13) of the Federal Reserve Act [D62][D82]. The 2023 report also flagged stablecoins as a funding-risk vulnerability, with stablecoin assets around $125 billion and potential to amplify strains in short-term funding markets [D7]. In 2024, the emphasis shifted toward research and monitoring: staff research covered stablecoins, tokenization, crypto-assets, and AI in payments, with engagement with the BIS, G7, FSB, and other central banks [D3]. The 2022 report also documented CBDC research (Box 5.4), including the Board's Technology Lab work and the Boston Fed/MIT Project Hamilton conclusion, and FSB work on global stablecoin arrangements and an international crypto-asset regulatory framework [D48][D4][D5].

2023: Interagency joint statement (Jan. 3, 2023) on key crypto risks including fraud, legal uncertainty, volatility, runs on stablecoins, and interconnectedness; second statement (Feb. 23, 2023) on crypto liquidity risk [D1][D61][D62].

data.answer:
The Federal Reserve is actively implementing the GENIUS Act (Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act) by proposing a comprehensive regulatory framework for payment stablecoins, rescinding older restrictive supervisory guidance, and conducting extensive research on the monetary and financial stability implications of stablecoin adoption. The Board’s most recent action, on September 24, 2026, was to request public comment on two proposals that would establish the core prudential and application requirements for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers [D56].

### Regulatory and Supervisory Actions

The Fed’s regulatory approach has shifted from cautious supervision to active rulemaking under the GENIUS Act, which was signed into law in July 2025 [D66][D87]. Key actions include:

*   **Proposed Regulatory Framework (September 24, 2026):** The Board requested public comment on two proposals to establish a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers [D56].
    *   **Proposal 1:** Requires full backing of stablecoins with permissible reserve assets (e.g., short-term Treasury bills, high-quality liquid assets), establishes standardized capital requirements for credit and operational risks, sets risk management standards, introduces safekeeping rules, and clarifies the permissibility of stablecoin activities for Board-supervised banks [D56].
    *   **Proposal 2:** Establishes a tailored application process for Board-supervised banks seeking to issue payment stablecoins, including requirements for business plans and financial information, as well as a process for appeals, hearings, and final determinations [D56].
*   **Customer Identification Program (June 18, 2026):** The Board, jointly with four other agencies, requested comment on a proposal requiring certain payment stablecoin issuers to maintain an effective customer identification program comparable to bank and credit union requirements [D60].
*   **Rescission of Older Guidance (April 24, 2025):** The Board withdrew its 2022 supervisory letter requiring advance notification of bank crypto-asset activities and its 2023 supervisory nonobjection process for dollar token activities, stating these actions ensure expectations remain aligned with evolving risks and support innovation [D78].
*   **Supervisory Priorities:** Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman testified in February 2026 that the Fed is working with other banking regulators to develop capital and liquidity regulations for stablecoin issuers as required by the GENIUS Act and is providing clarity on the treatment of digital assets to encourage responsible innovation [D57].

### Research on Monetary Policy and Financial Stability

Fed officials and staff have published extensive research analyzing how stablecoins could affect the economy, with a focus on monetary policy, bank deposits, and financial stability.

**Monetary Policy and Money Supply**
*   **Neutral Interest Rate (r*):** Governor Stephen Miran (November 2025) argued that stablecoins could become a "multitrillion dollar elephant in the room," with Fed staff estimates projecting $1–3 trillion in stablecoin uptake by the end of the decade [D75][D76]. This growth would boost demand for U.S. Treasury bills and other dollar liquid assets, potentially lowering the neutral interest rate (r*) by up to 40 basis points [D75][D77].
*   **Monetary Aggregates:** A September 2026 FEDS Note by Payne and Styczynski found that payment stablecoins are not currently included in U.S. monetary aggregates [D69]. Depending on their primary use, they could be classified as M1 (if used as a medium of exchange) or non-M1 M2 (if used as a store of value), though measurement challenges exist regarding double-counting of reserve assets and geographic scope [D69][D85][D86].

**Banking System and Deposits**
*   **Deposit Disintermediation:** Research indicates the impact on bank deposits depends critically on how stablecoin issuers manage reserves [D88]. If issuers hold reserves as bank deposits, aggregate deposits may remain largely unchanged but shift toward concentrated, uninsured wholesale deposits [D88][D89]. If reserves are held in Treasury bills or if issuers gain access to Federal Reserve master accounts paying interest, bank deposits could fall substantially, leading to greater disintermediation [D89][D90].
*   **Bank Adaptation:** A May 2026 FEDS Note by Hempel, Perez-Sangimino, and Wang noted that historically, banks have adapted to disintermediation threats (e.g., from money market funds and PayPal) through regulatory advocacy, product innovation, and strategic participation in the new ecosystem [D72][D24].

**Financial Stability**
*   **Run Risk and Reserve Quality:** Governor Michael Barr (March 2026) emphasized that stablecoins are "stable only if they can be reliably and promptly redeemed at par in a wide range of conditions," highlighting the critical importance of reserve asset quality and liquidity [D91]. He noted that the GENIUS Act’s requirement for 1:1 backing in safe, liquid assets is the primary mitigation tool, but implementation details regarding capital, liquidity, and anti-money laundering controls remain key concerns [D91][D92].
*   **Structural Vulnerabilities:** An April 2026 FEDS Note by Carapella, Lubis, and Vardoulakis identified three structural vulnerabilities: complex intermediation chains creating contagion risk, vertical integration complicating risk assessment, and accelerating retail adoption [D96][D97][D98]. The stablecoin market capitalization reached $317 billion as of April 6, 2026, representing more than 50% growth since early 2025 [D97].

### Historical Context

The Fed’s approach has evolved significantly since 2022:
*   **2022:** The Board issued SR 22-6/CA 22-6, requiring supervised banks to determine the legality of crypto-asset activities and notify the Fed before engaging in them [D51][D64].
*   **2023:** The Fed launched the Novel Activities Supervision Program with dedicated staff for crypto-assets and distributed ledger technology [D53][D61]. It also issued interagency statements on crypto risks, including runs on stablecoins, and established a supervisory nonobjection process for dollar token activities [D1][D61][D62].
*   **2024:** The focus shifted toward research and monitoring, with staff studying stablecoins, tokenization, and AI in payments, while engaging with international bodies like the BIS and FSB [D3].

This evolution reflects a transition from initial caution and notification requirements to a more structured, rule-based framework designed to integrate stablecoins into the financial system while managing associated risks.

question: What do Fed and New York Fed data say about the state of household finances?
answer:
Taking "Fed and New York Fed data" to mean the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF), the Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking (SHED) "Economic Well-Being" report, and the New York Fed's Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit: the data paint a picture of a household sector that is **wealthy and low-leveraged on balance sheets, but with financial well‑being that is stable yet below pre‑pandemic peaks, and with credit stress increasingly concentrated among struggling households.** The most recent data (2026:Q2 debt report; 2025 SHED) show debt growing modestly, delinquencies on existing balances ticking up, and credit card balance growth sharply concentrated among those "finding it difficult to get by."

## 1. Wealth and income (SCF, 2019→2022)
The latest triennial SCF (2022 survey, published October 2023) shows broad-based gains, led by housing:
- **Net worth:** Real median family net worth rose 37% to $192,700 (from $141,140 in 2019); mean rose 23% to $1,059,470 (from $865,720). The median jump was the largest three‑year increase in SCF history, implying some narrowing of the wealth distribution [D5][D19].
- **Housing wealth:** Homeownership rose slightly to 66.1%; median net housing value (home value minus home‑secured debt) jumped from $139,100 to $201,000, while the median primary residence value rose to $323,000 (from $260,820). Affordability fell to historic lows, with the median home worth 4.6× median family income [D6][D24].
- **Financial assets:** Median financial‑asset holdings among holding families rose 29% to $38,840 (from $30,140) [D20][D21].
- **Income:** Real median family income grew a modest 3% to $70,259 (from $68,454); mean income grew 15% to $141,390, with growth concentrated at the top [D5][D22].
- **By age:** The youngest families (<35) saw the largest median net‑worth gain (+140%, to $39,040); the oldest (75+) the smallest (+13%, to $334,700), and median income fell slightly for 75+ (−3%) [D19][D22].

## 2. Debt and credit (NY Fed, 2026:Q2)
The New York Fed's Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit (released August 11, 2026) shows total debt growing modestly, with consumer credit outpacing mortgages:
- **Total household debt:** $18.77 trillion in 2026:Q2, up 2.1% from $18.39 trillion in 2025:Q2 [D9].
- **By type (2026:Q2, YoY change):** Mortgage $13.12T (+1.4%); auto loans $1.71T (+3.5%); credit cards $1.26T (+4.5%); home‑equity revolving $0.46T (+11.6%); student loans $1.65T (+0.8%); other consumer credit $0.57T (+5.2%) [D9].
- **Delinquency (90+ days, share of balance):** Rose overall from 3.04% to 3.31% YoY, with increases across mortgages (0.82%→0.99%), auto (4.99%→5.49%), credit cards (12.27%→12.92%), and student loans (10.16%→10.60%) [D25].
- **New delinquency (30+ days):** Improved, falling from 5.26% to 4.95% overall, with student loans dropping sharply from 13.03% to 7.83%; new serious (90+) delinquency fell from 2.91% to 2.57% [D8][D23].

## 3. Economic well‑being (SHED, 2025)
The Federal Reserve's "Economic Well‑Being of U.S. Households in 2025" report (SHED fielded October 17–28, 2025; released May 13, 2026) finds well‑being stable but slightly below pre‑pandemic levels:
- **Overall:** 73% of adults reported doing okay or living comfortably (unchanged from 2024, below the 2021 high of 78%); 63% could cover a $400 emergency with cash or its equivalent (unchanged for three years, down from 68% in 2021) [D1][D4][D11].
- **Concerns:** Price increases remained the top concern (91% minor/major, unchanged), though the "major concern" share fell to 53% from 56%; job concerns rose to 42% from 37%, and layoffs ticked up to 7% from 6% [D1][D3].
- **Hardships:** 16% missed bills, 8% had food insufficiency, 26% skipped medical care (down from 28%), and 59% had a major unexpected expense [D4].
- **Credit stress concentrated among the struggling:** Since 2023, average credit card balances rose 37% ($2,530) for those "finding it difficult to get by" but only 1% ($59) for those "living comfortably"; the struggling groups accounted for 65% of balance growth (vs. ~40% in prior surveys) [D13][D14]. BNPL use edged up to 16%, and 23% of student‑loan borrowers had recent payment difficulty, mostly affordability‑driven [D10][D16].
- **Demographics:** Well‑being declined for young adults, low‑income families, and Black adults (down 5 points to 60%); 49% of under‑30s lived with a parent [D2][D3][D12].

## 4. Financial vulnerability (SCF, 2019→2022)
The SCF also shows a household sector with low leverage and strong ability to pay:
- The median leverage ratio (debt/assets) fell to a 20‑year low of 29.2%; the median payment‑to‑income ratio hit a record low of 13.4%; and the share of families declaring bankruptcy in the past five years fell to 1.3% [D7].
- Credit card debt was held by ~45% of families (stable), with median balances declining to $2,700; student debt was held by 22% of families (unchanged), with median balances around $25,000 [D7].

**Caveats on coverage:** The SCF figures are from the 2022 survey (the most recent triennial release, published 2023) and are in real 2022 dollars; the SHED reflects conditions at the time of the October 2025 fielding; and the NY Fed debt figures are as of 2026:Q2. The evidence does not include a more recent SCF (the next triennial would be 2025) or the NY Fed report's narrative prose, so the wealth/income picture is anchored to 2022 while the debt and well‑being picture is current through 2025–2026.

data.text: I have all the key information needed. Let me compile the findings.

data.answer:
The Federal Reserve's "Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025" report (SHED, fielded Oct 17–28, 2025; released May 13, 2026) found financial well-being stable but slightly below pre-pandemic levels. 73% of adults reported doing okay or living comfortably (unchanged from 2024, below the 2021 high of 78%), and 63% could cover a $400 emergency with cash or its equivalent (unchanged for three years, down from 68% in 2021). Price increases remained the top concern (91% minor/major, unchanged), though the "major concern" share fell to 53% from 56%. The labor market was solid but softening: job concerns rose to 42% from 37%, layoffs ticked up to 7% from 6%, and 15% of under-30s cited inability to find work. Income pressures eased slightly—58% said price changes worsened their finances, down from 60% (2024) and 65% (2023). Hardships were persistent: 16% missed bills, 8% had food insufficiency, 26% skipped medical care, and 59% had a major unexpected expense. On debt, credit card balance growth since 2023 has concentrated among struggling households (balances +37% for those "finding it difficult to get by" vs. +1% for those "living comfortably"); BNPL use edged up to 16%; and 23% of student-loan borrowers had recent payment difficulty, mostly affordability-driven. Well-being declined for young adults, low-income families, and Black adults (down 5 points to 60%).

For context, the "Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2019 to 2022" SCF report showed broad-based gains: real median family income rose 3% (mean +15%, with growth concentrated at the top), while real median net worth surged 37% (mean +23%)—the largest three-year median net worth jump in SCF history, implying some narrowing of the wealth distribution. Homeownership rose slightly to 66.1%, median net housing value jumped to $201,000, and housing affordability fell to historic lows (median home worth 4.6× median income). Debt burden eased: the median leverage ratio hit a 20-year low of 29.2%, the median payment-to-income ratio fell to a record low 13.4%, and bankruptcy declarations fell to 1.3%.

data.answer:
Taking "Fed and New York Fed data" to mean the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF), the Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking (SHED) "Economic Well-Being" report, and the New York Fed's Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit: the data paint a picture of a household sector that is **wealthy and low-leveraged on balance sheets, but with financial well‑being that is stable yet below pre‑pandemic peaks, and with credit stress increasingly concentrated among struggling households.** The most recent data (2026:Q2 debt report; 2025 SHED) show debt growing modestly, delinquencies on existing balances ticking up, and credit card balance growth sharply concentrated among those "finding it difficult to get by."

## 1. Wealth and income (SCF, 2019→2022)
The latest triennial SCF (2022 survey, published October 2023) shows broad-based gains, led by housing:
- **Net worth:** Real median family net worth rose 37% to $192,700 (from $141,140 in 2019); mean rose 23% to $1,059,470 (from $865,720). The median jump was the largest three‑year increase in SCF history, implying some narrowing of the wealth distribution [D5][D19].
- **Housing wealth:** Homeownership rose slightly to 66.1%; median net housing value (home value minus home‑secured debt) jumped from $139,100 to $201,000, while the median primary residence value rose to $323,000 (from $260,820). Affordability fell to historic lows, with the median home worth 4.6× median family income [D6][D24].
- **Financial assets:** Median financial‑asset holdings among holding families rose 29% to $38,840 (from $30,140) [D20][D21].
- **Income:** Real median family income grew a modest 3% to $70,259 (from $68,454); mean income grew 15% to $141,390, with growth concentrated at the top [D5][D22].
- **By age:** The youngest families (<35) saw the largest median net‑worth gain (+140%, to $39,040); the oldest (75+) the smallest (+13%, to $334,700), and median income fell slightly for 75+ (−3%) [D19][D22].

## 2. Debt and credit (NY Fed, 2026:Q2)
The New York Fed's Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit (released August 11, 2026) shows total debt growing modestly, with consumer credit outpacing mortgages:
- **Total household debt:** $18.77 trillion in 2026:Q2, up 2.1% from $18.39 trillion in 2025:Q2 [D9].
- **By type (2026:Q2, YoY change):** Mortgage $13.12T (+1.4%); auto loans $1.71T (+3.5%); credit cards $1.26T (+4.5%); home‑equity revolving $0.46T (+11.6%); student loans $1.65T (+0.8%); other consumer credit $0.57T (+5.2%) [D9].
- **Delinquency (90+ days, share of balance):** Rose overall from 3.04% to 3.31% YoY, with increases across mortgages (0.82%→0.99%), auto (4.99%→5.49%), credit cards (12.27%→12.92%), and student loans (10.16%→10.60%) [D25].
- **New delinquency (30+ days):** Improved, falling from 5.26% to 4.95% overall, with student loans dropping sharply from 13.03% to 7.83%; new serious (90+) delinquency fell from 2.91% to 2.57% [D8][D23].
- Note: the 2026:Q2 report includes a revision to 2026:Q1 credit card balances [D9].

## 3. Economic well‑being (SHED, 2025)
The Federal Reserve's "Economic Well‑Being of U.S. Households in 2025" report (SHED fielded October 17–28, 2025; released May 13, 2026) finds well‑being stable but slightly below pre‑pandemic levels:
- **Overall:** 73% of adults reported doing okay or living comfortably (unchanged from 2024, below the 2021 high of 78%); 63% could cover a $400 emergency with cash or its equivalent (unchanged for three years, down from 68% in 2021) [D1][D4][D11].
- **Concerns:** Price increases remained the top concern (91% minor/major, unchanged), though the "major concern" share fell to 53% from 56%; job concerns rose to 42% from 37%, and layoffs ticked up to 7% from 6% [D1][D3].
- **Hardships:** 16% missed bills, 8% had food insufficiency, 26% skipped medical care (down from 28%), and 59% had a major unexpected expense [D4].
- **Credit stress concentrated among the struggling:** Since 2023, average credit card balances rose 37% ($2,530) for those "finding it difficult to get by" but only 1% ($59) for those "living comfortably"; the struggling groups accounted for 65% of balance growth (vs. ~40% in prior surveys) [D10][D13][D14]. BNPL use edged up to 16%, and 23% of student‑loan borrowers had recent payment difficulty, mostly affordability‑driven [D10][D16].
- **Demographics:** Well‑being declined for young adults, low‑income families, and Black adults (down 5 points to 60%); 49% of under‑30s lived with a parent [D2][D3][D12].

## 4. Financial vulnerability (SCF, 2019→2022)
The SCF also shows a household sector with low leverage and strong ability to pay:
- The median leverage ratio (debt/assets) fell to a 20‑year low of 29.2%; the median payment‑to‑income ratio hit a record low of 13.4%; and the share of families declaring bankruptcy in the past five years fell to 1.3% [D7].
- Credit card debt was held by ~45% of families (stable), with median balances declining to $2,700; student debt was held by 22% of families (unchanged), with median balances around $25,000 [D7].

**Caveats on coverage:** The SCF figures are from the 2022 survey (the most recent triennial release, published 2023) and are in real 2022 dollars; the SHED reflects conditions at the time of the October 2025 fielding; and the NY Fed debt figures are as of 2026:Q2. The evidence does not include a more recent SCF (the next triennial would be 2025) or the NY Fed report's narrative prose, so the wealth/income picture is anchored to 2022 while the debt and well‑being picture is current through 2025–2026.
